title: Rare cancer cases strike in California community as families demand answers
summary: At least six children in Ladera Ranch, California, have been diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma, prompting environmental testing and a state health review.
story: Dr. Janet Yoon, a pediatric oncologist and sarcoma specialist at City of Hope in Los Angeles, shares her thoughts on a cluster of rare cancer diagnoses in Ladera Ranch, California.
A cluster of rare cancer diagnoses has sparked concern and prompted environmental testing in Ladera Ranch, California, although state health officials say no specific cause has been identified.
At least six children in the area have been diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma, according to federal officials and local reporting.
This exceptionally rare cancer, which forms in the bone or nearby soft tissue, primarily occurs in adolescents and young adults, per the National Cancer Institute.
WOMAN LOSES BEST FRIEND TO OVARIAN CANCER, THEN RECEIVES SAME DEVASTATING DIAGNOSIS MONTHS LATER

"Knowing that this is a very rare cancer diagnosis amplifies the concerns," Dr. Janet Yoon, a pediatric oncologist and sarcoma specialist at City of Hope in Los Angeles, told Fox News Digital. "Anytime you hear of cases in a geographic location, it does raise some concerns ... I can completely understand why further investigation is being done."

A cluster of rare cancer diagnoses has sparked concern and prompted environmental testing in Ladera Ranch, California, although state health officials say no specific cause has been identified. (iStock)

Following the March 2026 death of 17-year-old Brody Matteson from complications of treatment for Ewing sarcoma, more families began speaking publicly about rare cancer diagnoses in the community, according to local reports.
Community seeks answers

Some residents – including Matteson's father, Dustin Matteson – have suggested the illnesses could be linked to the community's use of herbicides and pesticides, which prompted calls for a broader environmental investigation.
"We don't have a clear line of evidence for pesticides, but it is one of the things that concerns us," Matteson said to NBC Los Angeles in July.
ALCOHOL TIED TO SURPRISING CANCER DEATH PATTERN IN ADULTS UNDER 55, RESEARCHERS FIND

In 2024, prompted by residents’ concerns, the California Department of Public Health conducted a county-level review in an attempt to determine whether pesticide use in the community could have played a role in the development of certain cancer types.
"That analysis did not find an unusual pattern at the county level, but the data available at the time was​ limited," the CDPH stated on its website.
The agency is now conducting a second review of cancer incidence data for the Ladera Ranch area.

Following the March 2026 death of 17-year-old Brody Matteson from complications of treatment for Ewing sarcoma, more families began speaking publicly about rare cancer diagnoses in the community, according to local reports. (Matteson family)

"CDPH currently estimates the assessment will be completed in fall 2026, although the timeline may change based on the scope and complexity of the review and any additional information that may need to be evaluated," the agency stated.
"At this time, our colleagues at CalEPA (California Environmental Protection Agency) and its boards, departments and offices have not identified any immediate environmental hazards."
"We don't have a clear line of evidence for pesticides, but it is one of the things that concerns us."

The CDPH stated that it is not yet known whether diagnoses of Ewing sarcoma and other cancer types are higher than expected in the Ladera Ranch community – or whether environmental factors can increase the risk.

In July 2026, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli asked the Environmental Protection Agency to investigate possible environmental factors that could have contributed to multiple pediatric cancer cases.
According to federal officials and local reporting, at least six children in the area have been diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma. (iStock)

Over the summer, hundreds of residents gathered at community meetings. At the same time, Ladera Ranch Maintenance Corporation (LARMAC) – the master homeowners association (HOA) for the planned community of Ladera Ranch in Orange County – temporarily paused its use of certain landscape chemicals and formed an advisory committee to review its landscaping practices.

As the investigation has continued, some residents have also publicly reported diagnoses of other cancers, including glioblastoma, although the current state review has not established whether those cases are related.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
On Sept. 14, California State Fullerton researchers began collecting soil and water samples from local parks as part of the environmental investigation.

Jennifer Piazza, Ph.D., professor in the Department of Public Health at Cal State Fullerton, assembled a team of researchers to help address the environmental concerns stemming from the pediatric cancer cases.
Some residents have suggested the illnesses could be linked to the community's use of herbicides and pesticides, which prompted calls for a broader environmental investigation. (iStock)

"Environmental sampling is the first step of our larger, ongoing scientific investigation," she told Fox News Digital. "We are collecting soil and water samples across Ladera Ranch. They are being analyzed for heavy metals, such as arsenic and lead, as well as pesticides."
The team expects to have results by the end of the year, Piazza said.
"I also want to emphasize that whatever we find does not imply causality in terms of the pediatric cancer cases in Ladera Ranch," she added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
LARMAC released a statement to People magazine, extending its "heartfelt compassion to the families who have been affected by these devastating illnesses."

"LARMAC takes these concerns seriously. We are aware that public health agencies are reviewing available information, and we will continue to cooperate with those efforts and follow guidance provided by the appropriate health and regulatory authorities."
"It's pain that persists. It's pain that wakes them up from their sleep. It's pain that limits their daily activities."

"At this time, we are not aware of any determination by those agencies identifying a specific environmental cause or linking the Association’s landscape management practices to these illnesses," the statement read.
The organization also noted that it has reduced the use of synthetic pesticides and switched to organic pesticides.
What to know about Ewing sarcoma
"With Ewing sarcoma, there is no confirmed genetic or environmental cause that we know of," Yoon told Fox News Digital.
"We have not found any confirmed genetic or environmental factor that increases the likelihood of developing Ewing sarcoma."
Ewing sarcoma most often presents as persistent pain rather than a typical sports injury or growing pain, according to an oncologist. (iStock)

Some studies have linked occupational or high-level exposure to certain pesticides with an increased risk of several cancers, although the evidence varies by chemical and cancer type, according to the American Cancer Society.
No known lifestyle-related or environmental cause of Ewing sarcoma has been identified, the ACS states.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The disease most often presents as persistent pain rather than a typical sports injury or growing pain, according to Yoon.
"It's pain that persists. It's pain that wakes them up from their sleep. It's pain that limits their daily activities."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The doctor called cancer the "great masquerader" in children due to its rarity. "Growing pains are much more common than cancer," she added.

Yoon encouraged families to seek medical evaluation if pain is persistent, worsening or interfering with normal activities. Specialized cancer centers with sarcoma expertise can help ensure an accurate diagnosis, she advised.

title: Pentagon unveils battlefield test to ensure new generals are warfighters – not Washington bureaucrats
summary: Pete Hegseth's Pentagon overhaul introduces wargame-style assessments requiring senior officers to solve combat problems before earning a star.
story: Stu Scheller tells Fox News Digital why the Pentagon wants officers to prove they can solve combat problems—not just build impressive careers—before they're promoted to general.

FIRST ON FOX: The Pentagon is raising the bar on who gets promoted to general by rolling out a new battlefield-style assessment requiring senior officers to demonstrate how they would solve complex military problems. It's the most significant change in decades for how future generals for every branch are selected.

Internal documents obtained by Fox News Digital show every military service has developed its own version of the new Joint Warfighting Evaluation (JWE), a standardized assessment intended to measure operational planning, decision-making and leadership under simulated combat conditions. The Pentagon says the assessment will supplement existing performance evaluations and become an additional metric considered by promotion boards beginning with the fiscal year 2027 cycle.

The effort grew out of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth's push to overhaul military evaluations and promotions, with a focus on identifying officers who can perform in combat rather than simply build strong career records.
PENTAGON FIRES BACK AFTER MARK KELLY ACCUSES PETE HEGSETH OF TARGETING WOMEN AND BLACK MILITARY OFFICERS

Senior military leaders listen as U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth speaks at Marine Corps Base Quantico on September 30, 2025 in Quantico, Virginia. In an unprecedented gathering, almost 800 generals, admirals and their senior enlisted leaders have been ordered into one location from around the world on short notice. (robynmac)

"People figure out they don't have to be the best at their job, they have to be the best at making sure their boss thinks they're the best," Stu Scheller, the senior Pentagon adviser leading the effort, told Fox News Digital. "And those are actually two very different things."
Under the current system, officers accumulate evaluations from their superiors throughout their careers that become a central part of the record considered by promotion boards.
'WOKE' MILITARY ACADEMIES TARGETED IN NEW BLUEPRINT FOR SWEEPING WARFIGHTING OVERHAUL

"Right now in our current system, we have people that are very good at navigating their careers," Scheller said. "We have very good, I want to be clear, very good military personnel and leaders across the military, but there isn't a stand-alone function that can truly assess the best military commanders on the battlefield."

Scheller said these performance reports will remain the "bedrock" of promotion decisions, while the JWE will give boards a separate measure of how well an officer can solve the kinds of military problems they could face in command.
What that assessment looks like will vary by service.

The Pentagon has developed six versions — one for each of the five military services and another through the Joint Staff — ranging from online simulations to hours-long, in-person wargames, the documents reviewed by Fox News Digital detail.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine speak to members of the media during a press briefing at the Pentagon in Washington, Tuesday, May 5, 2026. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP Photo)

In some versions, officers will be presented with a military problem and forced to make decisions as an AI-powered adversary reacts to their moves. Another will bring officers into a war college for an in-person wargame, where evaluators will watch how they respond as an enemy counters their decisions in real time.
"You make a move, enemy makes a move, how I react based on a time environment," Scheller said.

The service plans obtained by Fox News Digital show just how different the evaluations will be. The Army plans to put roughly 900 eligible colonels through a remote written assessment followed by a digital wargame, while roughly 1,330 Air Force colonels will take a two-hour online analysis test followed by a one-hour interactive simulation. The Space Force will use the same basic format for roughly 125 officers.

The Navy's version is considerably more intensive. Roughly 308 captains in the unrestricted line and information warfare communities will travel to the Naval War College for a three-hour written assessment followed by a two- to three-hour wargame. The Marine Corps plans an eight-hour remote evaluation for up to 175 colonels using an AI-enabled platform that combines written assessments with situational judgment tests.
Scheller cautioned that none of the exercises can perfectly recreate the pressures of actual combat and said the Pentagon expects to change the assessments as it learns what works.
"Ultimately, no matter how good we get at this, there's no one task that's gonna perfectly replicate war," he said. "We're not trying to come up with the perfect solution right out the gate."
COMMANDING GENERAL OF THE US ARMY IN EUROPEAN AND AFRICAN THEATER IS UNEXPECTEDLY STEPPING DOWN

Scheller stressed that the Pentagon is not replacing the existing promotion system. Performance reports and the rest of an officer's career record will continue to account for the bulk of the evaluation, while the JWE will provide promotion boards with an additional data point.
How heavily that new data point will be weighted has not yet been decided.
"The secretary still has judgment based on how it will be weighted in the board, so we haven't determined," Scheller said. "We're kind of waiting to see how well this thing is rolled out."

U.S. General Xavier T. Brunson, commander of the ROK/US Combined Forces Command (CFC), the United States Forces Korea (USFK) and the United Nations Command (UNC), walks on a pontoon bridge with U.S. and South Korean Army soldiers during a U.S.-South Korea joint river-crossing exercise, which is a part of the annual Freedom Shield joint military training, near the demilitarized zone separating South and North Korea, in Yeoncheon, South Korea, March 14, 2026. (Kim Soo-hyeon/Reuters)

The first real test will come next year. Eligible O-6s will undergo the evaluations between roughly February and June 2027, Scheller said, ahead of the services' O-7 promotion boards between July and September.

The Pentagon plans to study the results from that first cycle before determining how much influence the JWE should have on future promotion boards and how the assessments should evolve for the following year, according to the internal documents.
The new evaluation is the latest step in a broader overhaul of how the Pentagon selects, evaluates and retains its senior military leaders under Hegseth.

Hegseth told hundreds of generals and admirals last year that the military's promotion system was being "thoroughly reexamined," pledging to promote top performers faster, push out poor performers more quickly and turn evaluations, military education and field exercises into meaningful tests rather than "box checks."

He has also moved to shrink the upper ranks themselves, ordering a 20% reduction in active-duty four-star positions and a broader 10% cut in general and flag officer positions as part of a restructuring of military commands.
And Hegseth has taken a more direct role in deciding who receives a star.

Earlier this year, he removed several Navy captains from a list of officers selected by a promotion board for one-star admiral after previously intervening in an Army brigadier general promotion list. The Pentagon has said promotions under Hegseth will be based on merit.

Meanwhile, the unusual interventions have drawn criticism and concern from some lawmakers, military officers and outside analysts worried about political influence over the traditionally service-driven process.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The changes have come alongside significant turnover at the top of the military.

Trump and Hegseth have removed or replaced a number of senior leaders since the beginning of the administration, including former Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. CQ Brown and former Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Lisa Franchetti. Hegseth also forced out Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George this year before the scheduled end of his term.

title: Fox News Power Rankings: For the Democrats, where could it possibly go wrong?
summary: Democrats hold an 11-point generic ballot lead as Trump's Iran war drives gas prices up 50%, dragging down Republican midterm prospects nationwide.
story: A new poll indicates the MAGA movement and capitalism hold higher favorability among voters than the Democratic Socialists of America and socialism. Panelists Leslie Marshall and Matt Whitlock join 'America Reports' to debate the ideological direction of the Democratic Party. The discussion also addresses a recent Axios report concerning internal skepticism about former Vice President Kamala Harris running in the 2028 presidential election.
From the moment President Trump completed his comeback in 2024, voters had good reason to think that the Democrats would retake the House this November.

The president’s party has lost ground in all but two elections since 1934, including the two Trump-era midterms, where the party in power lost 40 seats (Republicans, 2018) and 9 seats (Democrats, 2022).
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOUSE CONTROL COULD HINGE ON WHETHER THE OLD POLITICAL RULES STILL APPLY
Fox News Power Rankings on midterm seat losses under President Donald Trump's economy. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
With Republicans currently hanging by a thread in the House, most of the work has already been done for Team Blue.
The number of seats that will change hands is another question, and here, Trump’s signature policies are playing a big role.
Fox News Power Rankings on Democrat lead in latest polling. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

As we enter fall, Democrats are enjoying their widest polling lead of the year. Voters say they prefer the Democrat to the Republican in their district by an average of 7 points in new polls (49%-42%).
LEE CARTER: THE SUMMER POLLS MISSED THE POINT: VOTERS ARE MOVING — AND THE MIDTERMS BEGIN
Fox News Power Rankings on Democrat party's polling. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
Democrats perform even better among likely voters with an 11-point average lead (53%-42%).
That’s a larger and more consistent lead than the GOP had this time four years ago.
These polls suggest that we’re heading for a "blue wave" like the one Democrats rode eight years ago.
(That wave probably won’t rise as high as it once did. Thanks to redistricting, there are fewer seats in play for either party, so think of a gain of a few dozen as the modern equivalent of 40.)
Still, there are six weeks until election day, and there are some things we don’t know. With all signs currently pointing to a good Democratic night, where could it possibly go wrong?
Will anything change on Iran?
The administration’s decision to go to war with Iran is proving costly for the GOP.
RECORD GAS PRICES SQUEEZE AMERICANS AS SUMMER TRAVEL SEASON ENDS, MIDTERMS LOOM AND IRAN WAR WAGES ON
Fox News Power Rankings on gas prices and polling trends. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
Gas prices sit at $4.48 today, up 50% from $2.98 at the start of the war, and increasing at a higher rate this month.
Trump’s worst ratings have been on inflation and the cost of living, and 61% of voters called gas prices a "major problem" in last week’s Fox News Poll.

Yesterday, Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson became the second Republican Senate candidate to call for an end to the war (the first was Sen. Susan Collins, in April). No doubt many vulnerable House GOP incumbents feel the same way.
In an election that looks less like an embrace of Democrats than a rejection of Trump’s agenda, a change of course in Iran would have an impact.
Could the DSA drag down the Democratic vote?

Democrats have presented voters with two economic visions: the first, championed by candidates like Abdul El-Sayed and Troy Jackson, calls for a revolution on healthcare and taxes. The other, more common and less sweeping, is largely about undoing the Trump agenda.
MORNING GLORY: FIVE SENATE RACES SHOW WHY DEMOCRATS MAY REGRET THEIR PRIMARY CHOICES
Fox News Power Rankings on candidate positions and voting trends. (Remy Numa/Fox News) (Fox News)

Voters say they like core parts of the progressive agenda, including raising taxes on billionaires, which makes voters more likely to vote for a candidate by a 34-point margin, according to a new NBC News Poll, and Medicare for All, which has a 17-point margin.
Fox News Power Rankings on candidate positions and voting trends. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

But the movements to which those policies are tied don’t fare as well: voters are less likely to support a candidate endorsed by Bernie Sanders by a 10-point margin, and less likely to vote for a candidate who supports the Democratic Socialists of America by 19 points.
We don’t know yet whether candidates on the left wing of the Democratic Party will be able to thread this needle.
Fox News Power Rankings on candidate positions and voting trends. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Trump’s economic messaging is broadly unpopular, according to the same poll, including his proposal to send $5,000 checks to voters if Republicans keep control of Congress, as well as sending funding and weapons to Israel. That’s what is likely to get Democrats over the line.
But watch whether the DSA hurts the Dems.
Are there more MAGA votes out there?
The Republicans’ midterm convention is now in the rear-view mirror, and it didn’t make a dent in the polls we’ve seen.
That probably wasn’t the goal for the GOP, who used the "Trumpapalooza" to remind loyal MAGA voters about the president’s wins on immigration and crime, among other issues.
How many of them will show up on election day?
Fox News Power Rankings on Trump endorsements. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

In last week’s Fox News Poll, a quarter of voters said an endorsement from President Trump makes them more likely to vote for a candidate. That quarter is mostly the MAGA base, and it’s large enough to impact a race.
MAGA turnout could limit the Democrats’ ceiling.
In this week’s Power Rankings, Kansas’ Senate race gets more competitive and seventeen House races shift towards the Democrats. Plus, updates in two gubernatorial races.
Senate: Kansas becomes the ninth battleground state
Democrats can celebrate a shift in the political environment, but every Senate race is different. It’s still a toss-up in this forecast.
Fox News Power Rankings on which party voters trust more to handle the economy. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
Each party has 47 seats, with six in the middle to determine control: Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, and Texas.
Races in the "lean" categories are highly competitive, too, and today, Kansas joins New Hampshire and North Carolina to round out the list of nine battleground states.

Kansas has been on the Democrats’ radar for most of the year, thanks to what they believe to be a star recruit in megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton. He is campaigning on gas and diesel prices, which have an outsize impact in the rural and agriculture-heavy Midwest.
Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News) (Fox News)

Sen. Roger Marshall, the incumbent, got some help last week from a star of the Republicans’ own: Vice President JD Vance, who rallied with Marshall to promote the Trump administration’s manufacturing agenda.
The state hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years, but it isn’t allergic to statewide Dems: incumbent governor Laura Kelly is one, and she won in both 2018 and 2022.
Kansas moves from Likely R to Lean R.
Meanwhile, in Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is consolidating support as he seeks a second term. His race moves from Lean D to Likely D.
Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
House: Democrats enjoy a higher ceiling; narrow pathways remain for a Republican majority
The Democrats have made bigger gains in the House, where this week’s set of polls has the most impact.
Fox News Power Rankings on House forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News) (Fox News)
The party has 215 seats in this forecast, which means they would only need to win 3 of the 19 toss-ups to flip the House.
On a "good night" for Democrats, which would see them win all of those toss-up races, they’d take up to 234 seats, leaving the Republicans with 201.
Fox News Power Rankings on House forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
Narrow pathways remain for the GOP. While this forecast sees an expansion of the Republican House majority as unlikely, a good night for the party would have them hold on to the House with 220 seats.

The shifts are largely a product of the generic ballot polling. The Democrats’ lead among likely voters of 8 to 13 points will be too much for GOP campaigns in some highly competitive areas to overcome. The same is true even for a few districts that Trump won by a healthy margin two years ago.
Fox News Power Rankings on House forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
These changes also reflect the shift among Hispanic voters towards Democrats: from D+12 in the 2024 presidential race to D+29 in Fox’s latest generic ballot survey.

That will make a difference across Florida, where seven races shift towards Democrats, including the 25th district (held by Jared Moskowitz (D), from Toss-up to Lean D), and the 27th district (held by María Elvira Salazar (R), from Likely R to Lean R). It also impacts Texas, where the 34th district, held by Vicente Gonzalez (D), moves from Toss-up to Lean D.
Republicans are running strong campaigns in many of these districts, but if the Dems’ generic ballot advantage lasts, the party’s ceiling could get higher.
Fox News Power Rankings on House forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
Governor: Texas and Alaska drift away from the GOP

Data centers continue to play a major role in gubernatorial races across the country, especially in Ohio, where Fox’s Madison Alworth spoke to voters about the costs of data center construction yesterday, and in Texas, where incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott faces his toughest reelection challenge yet.
Fox News Power Rankings on gubernatorial forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
Abbott’s competitor, Democratic candidate and State Rep. Gina Hinojosa, has put the issue at the forefront of both of their campaigns.
Yesterday, Abbott widened his moratorium on data centers, with the construction of new centers now "effectively halted" until at least December.
The governor has important structural advantages as he seeks a fourth term, but polls keep showing a close race. Texas moves from Likely R to Lean R.
Fox News Power Rankings on gubernatorial forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
Finally, to Alaska, where new polling shows a close race for Senate, and what at first glance looks like a wide-open race for governor, with the Democrat ahead of three Republican candidates.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

When the GOP candidates are combined, the party runs even with the Democrat in this poll. But Alaska is one of two states with ranked choice voting. If more Democrats mark their second, third and fourth choices than Republicans, it could hurt the GOP’s chances of holding on to the 49th State. It moves from Lean R to Toss-up.
Rémy Numa is the lead political affairs specialist for Fox News Channel. You can follow him on Twitter: @remynuma.

title: George W Bush raises money for Republicans, but not key Senate candidate
summary: George W. Bush hosted a fundraiser for Senate Republicans but notably excluded Ken Paxton, who defeated Bush's nephew in the 2022 Texas primary.
story: Texas GOP U.S. Senate nominee Ken Paxton discusses the impact of the 2026 RNC midterm convention and his Democratic opponent James Talarico seemingly distancing himself from past views on ‘Hannity.’
Former President George W. Bush is helping fundraise for Republicans, but not the one who defeated his nephew, George P. Bush, in the 2022 Republican primary for Texas attorney general.

Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, held a fundraiser Monday night for Maintain the Majority with the former president as a "special guest," The New York Times reported. The event did not include GOP Senate candidate and current Texas AG Ken Paxton, who defeated Cornyn in this year's primary.

Maintain the Majority is a PAC that lists Cornyn along with Sens. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska; Jon Husted, R-Ohio, Susan Collins, R-Maine; Michigan Sen.-nominee Mike Rogers, New Hampshire Sen.-nominee John E. Sununu; and Iowa Sen.-nominee Ashley Hinson as joint fund participants, Minnesota Republican Sen.-nominee Michele Tafoya was a late addition to the Monday night event, according to the Times.

Notably absent on that list are Paxton, Republican North Carolina Sen.-nominee Mike Collins and Republican North Carolina Sen.-nominee Michael Whatley, a trio of Senate candidates closely tied to Trump's political orbit.
TRUMP FLEXES HIS POLITICAL MUSCLE OVER GOP AS DEMOCRATS SEE MIDTERM OPENING IN KEY RED STATE

Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has President Donald Trump's backing and access to his midterm $415 million war chest, but the New York Times notes former President George W. Bush and ousted Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, are not fundraising for him. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
Bush and Cornyn have long had a complicated relationship with President Donald Trump and his favored candidates, like Paxton.
Karl Rove, a former senior presidential advisor to Bush, recently declared he would vote for a Texas Democrat, too.
THUNE-ALIGNED GROUPS UNLEASH HISTORIC WAR CHEST TO DEFEND SENATE MAJORITY: 'WINNING MESSAGE'

Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, lost his battle against President Donald Trump-endorsed Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and now apparently is not including his GOP rival in his fundraising events. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images;)

"Early voting in Texas starts Monday, October 19, 2026 (28 days from today, September 21)," a Cornyn X post on Monday morning read, notably leaving out a mention of Paxton. "It runs through Friday, October 30. The 2026 midterms (Election Day) are Tuesday, November 3, 2026 — 43 days from today."

While the PAC funds might not include Paxton, Trump's own midterm campaign war chest at MAGA Inc. — now under the watchful eye of former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt — has more than $415 million cash on hand, according to the latest FEC filing reported Sunday.
Michigan, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine and Alaska are all rated toss-ups in the latest Fox News Power Rankings in the race to hold the Republican's slim 53-47 Senate majority.

Democrats are looking at flipping seats against Collins, Husted, Sullivan, Hinson in Iowa, Whatley in North Carolina and Paxton in Texas. Republicans are eyeing potential pickups in Michigan, New Hampshire and Georgia.
REPUBLICAN CAVALRY ARRIVES FOR KEN PAXTON AS BIG-BUCKS TEXAS OFFENSIVE OPENS CASH FLOODGATES
Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

While midterms are historically unfavorable to the political party seated in the White House, Republicans holding the Senate could help tamp down Democrat momentum in Trump's final two years in office if the slim 218-214 Republican House majority is lost.

While Cornyn's establishment Republican coffers might not be made available to the man who ousted him in the primary, Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters has been confident that Texas' Senate seat will remain in the GOP's hands.

"You got to remember Ken Paxton won this state a couple of times in the general – he won a primary against a strong incumbent that's been there for a long time by a couple hundred thousand votes," Gruters told Fox News Digital last month.

"People want this race to be the biggest race in the country, but it really won't be because, at the end of the day, Paxton has proven time and time again that he's a winner; he's a winner in this state. Texas is ruby red," Gruters said. "Texas is a hardcore Republican state. They're going to send up a MAGA warrior because we have a lot of work to do, including passing the Save America Act."
JOHN THUNE GOES 'ALL IN' FOR KEN PAXTON AFTER BITTER PRIMARY RIPPED GOP APART
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While Texas is seeing California liberals flock to the state, Gruters predicted Paxton's statewide campaign strength is going to hold against Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico.

"Texas is a massive state, a lot resources from California are pouring in because these California liberals like Talafreako, but I don't think it's going to help him at the end of the day," Gruters added. "Paxton is going to win this race."
