title: Oil prices tumble to 2-week low on hopes for critical pipeline reopening and Iran diplomacy
summary: Oil prices fell sharply fell for a fifth straight trading session, reaching a two-week low on hopes of a renewed diplomatic push to end the Iran war and optimism over the reopening of a critical pipeline in Saudi Arabia.
story: Oil prices fell sharply fell for a fifth straight trading session, reaching a two-week low on hopes of a renewed diplomatic push to end the Iran war and optimism over the reopening of a critical pipeline in Saudi Arabia.
Brent crude oil briefly slipped below $98 per barrel while U.S. crude oil fell below $93 per barrel, their lowest prices since Sept. 8.
Prices first began sliding overnight on reports that Iran was offering to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days if the U.S. takes steps toward easing pressure on the country.
NBC News has not confirmed the reports. Iran’s semiofficial Fars news agency said that “Iranian sources have described these reports as unreliable and untrue,” without naming those sources.

It was the latest hint that there may be a window for Washington and Tehran to re-engage in their standoff over the Strait of Hormuz — a possibility that would be welcome relief for markets eager for the restoration of energy supplies from the Middle East.
President Donald Trump is holding a number of meetings with world leaders Tuesday at the United National General Assembly in New York City.

Trump signaled a willingness to meet with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, which had already soothed some market concerns. Asked about a potential meeting between the two leaders, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told NBC News, “I don’t think anything is scheduled at this point.”
Rubio added that the U.S. was “open to something like that,” though.

Since the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran war Feb. 28, vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has at times ground to a near halt. Over the course of the last week, daily traffic did not exceed 20 ships in a day, according to data from MarineTraffic.
Also fueling oil’s downward move Tuesday were reports about Saudi Arabia’s key east-west pipeline, which has effectively acted as a Strait of Hormuz workaround for oil exports.

On Sept. 11, the Saudi Energy Ministry said that the pipeline was shut after “multiple attacks” on it amid the escalating conflict with the Iran-backed Houthi rebels. Initially, experts worried that this closure could last months.

Reuters reported that the pipeline had already restarted, and could resume exports from a Red Sea port later in the day, citing three people familiar with the matter. Bloomberg News reported that Saudi Arabia was running tests on the pipeline with the hope of restarting it this week, citing multiple people familiar with the matter.
Saudi Aramco, which operates the pipeline, did not immediately respond to a request for comment from NBC News.

On NBC’s “TODAY,” Rubio said regarding prices, “if you look at the increases we’ve seen in just the last two weeks, the enormous majority of that increase is because the Houthi’s attacked a Saudi pipeline and the Saudis had to shut down that pipeline.”

“So there’s still oil in the system, but the markets are reacting to the expectation that there will not be as much Saudi oil in the future” as a result of the pipeline attack, Rubio added. “That is problem as well, which we are confronting here.”
Both oil benchmarks are elevated by more than 60% since the start of the year. So are retail gas prices, which as of Tuesday morning reached $4.47 per gallon. That’s up 50% since the Iran war began.
The price of diesel has also skyrocketed.

The national average hit a new all-time high of $6.52 per gallon Tuesday, up 82% since the start of year on a record run propelled in part by intensifying aerial attacks between Russia and Ukraine. Trump is set to hold talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday as he pushes for an energy truce.

Along with tumbling oil prices, bond yields also fell early Tuesday. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield, which heavily influences consumer borrowing rates, fell to as low as 4.92%, after reaching as high as 5.04% a week ago. That was its highest level since 2007.
The 30-year Treasury yield also dipped to as low as 5.25% Tuesday morning. Last week, it rose as high as 5.4%, a level it also last touched in 2007.
Global stocks rallied as well. The European-wide Stoxx 600 index rose more than 0.5%, as did Germany’s benchmark DAX and France CAC 40 indexes.

U.S. stock futures rose slightly but S&P 500 futures were largely flat, while Nasdaq 100 futures rose 0.2%. Those rises came after both indexes posted their best days since August on Monday, driven by falling oil prices.

title: U.S. military leaders divided over action against the Houthis
summary: WASHINGTON — U.S. military leaders are divided on whether President Donald Trump should get involved with the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, according to two U.S. officials.
story: WASHINGTON — U.S. military leaders are divided on whether President Donald Trump should get involved with the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, according to two U.S. officials.

The Saudis have been asking Trump for the U.S. military to take action against the Houthis, a request that grew more urgent in recent days as the rebels claimed they shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet and were quickly advancing on Marib province, which is home to Yemen’s largest oil and gas fields.

Some military leaders are making the case within the Pentagon and to Trump administration officials that opening another military front in the region is a bad idea amid concerns about the Pentagon’s dwindling supply of defensive and long-range weaponry, while noting that the Houthis are not striking U.S. ships, the U.S. officials said.

Yet other military leaders are arguing in favor of strikes, saying the U.S. should help Riyadh retaliate for Houthi strikes in Saudi Arabia and the claim of downing of the F-15 — a challenge to Saudi air superiority over Yemen, the officials said. They said these military leaders are privately expressing concern that for the U.S. not to act more forcefully is a betrayal of an important regional ally.

Trump had ordered strikes against the Houthis to begin around 5 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on Sunday, but the military was notified shortly after 2 p.m. on Sunday that the order was canceled, the two U.S. officials said. One of the officials said Trump has not taken military action off the table in the future.

One senior U.S. military leader in the region specifically warned that action against the Houthis could create unmitigated risk to U.S. troops in Middle East and the Iran war mission, including a U.S. naval blockade and security operations in the Strait of Hormuz, the two U.S. officials said. They said the military leader also made clear that U.S. forces could carry out the Iran mission and strikes against the Houthis and mitigate some of the risks, the officials said.

The internal divide underscores the bind the president is increasingly in as the U.S. remains locked in a war with Iran that he began but has struggled to end, and faces a shortage of key weaponry. The Saudis have been a critical U.S. ally in the Middle East, including throughout the war with Iran. Trump told Fox News over the weekend that he’s deciding whether to escalate the war with Iran, a position he has articulated on and off over the past few months.
The White House and a spokesperson for the Saudi Embassy in Washington, D.C., did not respond to a request for comment. The Pentagon declined to comment.

There has already been tension between the U.S. and its Middle East allies over the war. In May, Saudi Arabia was surprised by an announcement by Trump to help ships through the Strait of Hormuz and suspended the U.S. military’s ability to use its bases and airspace. Trump abruptly reversed his decision.

The U.S. has already been supporting the Saudis by sharing intelligence, helping with planning, sending military advisers forward with the Saudi forces and even providing some logistical support, NBC News has reported. But the Saudis have repeatedly asked the U.S. to do more, including help with strikes against the Houthis.

Trump had not shown interest in acting until Thursday, when Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman told him in a phone call that the kingdom cannot succeed alone and after a series of developments — including the Houthis targeting Saudi infrastructure, downing the F-15 and threatening to take control of Yemen’s oil industry, according to one of the U.S. officials.

After the call, Trump ordered the military to provide him with fresh options for strikes against the Houthis, the official said. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Dan Caine called a 6 p.m. emergency meeting in The Tank, the top-security conference room in the Pentagon, to discuss options, the official said, canceling a trip to Copenhagen to meet with NATO chiefs of defense.

U.S. military officials have presented Trump with options for degrading Houthi military capabilities and stopping the rebels’ recent advances several times since Thursday, the official said, adding that the Pentagon has enough assets in the region to be ready to act if ordered to do so.
The New York Times reported some details of Trump’s decision-making process.

Violence escalated over the weekend, as the Houthis said they’d used missiles and drones on Saturday to attack “sensitive” sites in ‌Riyadh and an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key oil export hub.

The spokesperson for the coalition forces issued a statement on Saturday saying Saudi Arabia had successfully intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Riyadh and that the Houthis “target civilians and civilian infrastructure in the capital.”

The militant group also made a rapid advance to control the Bab el Mandeb Strait on the Red Sea, yet another oil chokepoint. The advance has posed a major challenge for the Saudis, who rely on that shipping route particularly since the Strait of Hormuz has been largely shuttered during the Iran war.
The Houthis took control of Yemen in a bloody civil war in 2014 against a Saudi-backed coalition. A fragile truce between the Houthis and the Yemeni government backed by the U.N. was reached in 2022.

Trump announced a ceasefire with the Houthis last year after weeks of punishing strikes against the militant group. Under the deal, the U.S. suspended military action and the Houthis stopped attacking U.S. ships.

Trump recently has said his administration has had discussions with the Houthis but has not offered details. “The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said earlier this month. “They would much prefer not having us involved.”

title: Marco Rubio defends Trump’s ban on media outlets from White House, arguing police or soldiers are not ‘kicking down the doors’
summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the Trump administration’s decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, saying in an interview on NBC’s “TODAY” that President Donald Trump was not closing outlets or arresting reporters.
story: Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the Trump administration’s decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, saying in an interview on NBC’s “TODAY” that President Donald Trump was not closing outlets or arresting reporters.

“We’re not closing CNN,” Rubio said. “There aren’t a bunch of police officers or soldiers kicking down the doors of MSNBC or MS NOW, whatever it’s called, and arresting people and unplugging it from the grid. They’re just not allowed to work from the workspace at the White House.”
Trump’s ban on the media outlets marked the president’s most extreme instance so far of blocking access for news organizations whose coverage he dislikes.

The three banned outlets sued the Trump administration on Monday over the ban, and major television networks, including NBC News, have refused to provide TV pool coverage of the president at least through Monday. That coverage allows media members and subscribers to share video, editorial information and costs for newsworthy events where space is limited.
Television pool coverage of other administration officials, including Rubio, has continued. On Monday, CNN provided TV pool coverage of the secretary.
When asked by host Craig Melvin whether Rubio planned to make changes to his pool coverage, the secretary said, “We haven’t discussed it.”

Rubio told “TODAY” that the three banned outlets would be able to continue covering the president, adding that Trump believed that the outlets have shown bias against his administration and therefore did not have a right to remain in the White House building.
“What he is arguing is, why should I have these people, what right do they have to be embedded in this building?” Rubio said. “They can cover the White House. They just can’t have a desk there.”

In their lawsuit, the outlets argued that the ban violated their due process and First Amendment rights, claiming the ban “retaliates against protected newsgathering and speech” and bars the outlets “from a nonpublic forum for unlawful reasons.”

In his Truth Social announcement of the ban last week, Trump said the move was “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” In a separate post on Monday, Trump again criticized media as “fake news,” calling it “a threat to our National Security” that “must be stopped.”

title: Poll: Most voters say Trump has hurt the economy as competitive midterm election looms
summary: President Donald Trump’s sinking ratings threaten to drag down Republicans in November’s midterm elections, as voters blame him for high prices and a shaky economy, according to a new NBC News poll.
story: President Donald Trump’s sinking ratings threaten to drag down Republicans in November’s midterm elections, as voters blame him for high prices and a shaky economy, according to a new NBC News poll.

The president’s approval rating stands at 41% among registered voters, a second-term low in the poll, with a majority (55%) of voters saying they believe Trump’s policies have hurt the economy. That’s up from 48% in March, before the Iran war pushed up prices on gas and other goods and cemented the rising cost of living as voters’ most pressing issue.

title: No criminal charges in death of Nolan Wells, grand jury finds
summary: A grand jury will not pursue criminal charges in the death of Nolan Wells, the local district attorney said, forcefully rejecting months of speculation that race played a role in the death of the Mississippi teen this summer.
story: A grand jury will not pursue charges in the death of Nolan Wells, the local district attorney said Monday, forcefully rejecting months of speculation that race played a role in the death of the Mississippi teenager this summer.

District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath made the announcement in a video message, saying the grand jury returned a “no true bill,” meaning it did not find sufficient evidence to indict anyone with a crime. A partially redacted copy of the grand jury report was also posted to the DA’s Facebook page.

Wells, 18, was with friends celebrating July Fourth and was last seen on Horn Island, a barrier reef off Mississippi accessible only by boat. His body was found at the northwestern tip of the island July 6, his family’s lawyer said.

“There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan’s disappearance and death were racially motivated,” Myers McIlrath said. “Nolan’s friends loved Nolan, and Nolan loved them. Nolan chose to stay on the island that day, and there is not a scintilla of evidence to contradict that.”
The family’s lawyer, civil rights attorney Ben Crump, previously called into question whether race was a factor in Wells’ death, as it appeared Wells was one of a few Black people there that day.
On Monday, Myers McIlrath took direct aim at Crump and his team, saying they also previously informed her office that they’d found no evidence a crime had been committed against Wells.
“I’m not suggesting that a grieving mother police the rumors surrounding her child’s death,” the DA said. “What I am suggesting is that the Crump team knew better but did not do better.”
Crump in turn said a statement Tuesday, “This grand jury result leaves us with more questions than answers. Nolan’s family will not rest until we know what happened to him, and neither will we.”

“Mississippi’s own pathologist found two bruises on the back of this young man’s head ... An independent autopsy documented traces of blood and recent blunt force injuries to the back of Nolan’s head and his back. To this day, not one person has explained how they got there,” he added.
“We don’t know how Nolan died, and neither does the State of Mississippi. Mississippi must keep investigating,” Crump said. Wells’ parents are expected to make a public address later Tuesday.
State completes autopsy of Mississippi teen Nolan Wells
The grand jury issued 132 subpoenas and heard from 43 witnesses, and seven people were invited to testify before the panel, according to the partially redacted report.

It was made up of 23 grand jurors from a “cross section of citizens” from Jackson County between 27 and 68 of age, it said. Among them were 13 men and 10 women, including “12 Caucasians, five African Americans, one Asian, two Hispanics, two Native Americans and one individual who preferred ‘other,’” it said.

“The grand jury finds no credible evidence to support the public allegations that any persons who rode to or from Horn Island on July 4, 2026 ... engaged in any criminal conduct related to ​the death of Mr. Wells,” the report released by McIlrath’s office said.

Wells was last seen sometime in the afternoon of July 4. Friends told police that they had to leave early because their boat started taking on water but that Wells chose to stay and catch a ride back later with others.

The grand jury report found that it was common for people on Horn Island to “socialize on boats and in the water,” and that it was “not unusual or suspicious” for people to return from the island on different boats.

It concluded there was no evidence that Wells had any sort of physical altercation or argument with anyone the day he was last seen. It added “that the position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr. Wells’ body is consistent with drowning.”

Crump and Wells’ family have previously rejected notions that he drowned, saying he was athletic and a good swimmer. An independent autopsy commissioned by the family’s legal team found that the teenager’s cause and manner of death were “undetermined.”

The state’s chief medical examiner and a forensic pathologist retained by Wells’ family both “opined that the cause and manner of Mr. Wells’ death is undetermined and that drowning is a diagnosis of exclusion,” according to the grand jury report. It noted, however, that neither has ruled out accidental drowning as a cause.
Wells’ funeral July 20 attracted hundreds of people.

“Your absence has left an emptiness that can never truly be filled,” his mother, Christine Wells-Wonsley, said at the time. “In a world that can often feel dark, be like Nolan, be the light that brightens the lives of those around you.”

title: ‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular charged with rape in Massachusetts
summary: The “looksmaxxing” personality known as Clavicular has been charged with rape in Massachusetts, online court records show.
story: The “looksmaxxing” personality known as Clavicular has been charged with rape in Massachusetts, online court records show.

The charges listed against Clavicular, 20, whose real name is Braden Peters, are one count of rape, one count of drugging someone for sexual intercourse, and one count of procuring liquor for someone under 21 years old, according to the records.
The charges were filed Sept. 8, and the alleged offenses occurred May 23, 2025, the records indicate. More details about the allegations were not immediately available.
Online court records did not show an attorney who could speak on his behalf Monday night.

The Bulwark first reported the charges. A representative for Clavicular, Mitchell Jackson, said the outlet was “exaggerating” in its report and that Clavicular had not been served with an arrest warrant.
“Braden Peters has not been physically served. As usual the Bulwark is exaggerating,” Jackson said in a text message Monday night.
An email to the general mailbox of The Bulwark seeking comment was not immediately returned late Monday.
An arraignment was scheduled for Oct. 14, according to the court records.

Clavicular has gained internet fame — and notoriety — for a trend among young men known as “looksmaxxing,” which Meriam-Webster Dictionary recently called, “The practice of taking one or more sometimes extreme or dangerous measures intended to increase one’s physical attractiveness.”

He has been known for “bone smashing,” or using a hammer to intentionally break facial bones so they grow back stronger or looking better. The trend has been called potentially unhealthy and dangerous by experts.
Clavicular in April was sued by a teenage influencer in Florida who accused him of battery.

Aleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza, who online is known as Alorah or Alorah Ziva, filed a lawsuit in Miami-Dade County that alleged that in 2025 he arranged for her to go to Cape Cod, Massachusetts, gave her vodka until she was drunk, and then had sex with her while she was intoxicated, NBC South Florida reported.
Online court records do not indicate whether the charges of rape, drugging or procurement of alcohol to someone under 21 are related to the allegations in the lawsuit.
Clavicular’s attorney at the time said that he denies the allegations and “intends to vigorously defend himself,” according to the news station.

Clavicular and two other people in April were also charged in Florida with shooting at an alligator. He and another person pleaded no contest to unlawfully discharging a firearm in public and were given six months of probation and ordered to serve 20 hours of community service, according to NBC South Florida.

He was also hospitalized in April in Miami after a suspected overdose. He said in a livestream at the time after being released from the hospital that, “I ain’t gonna be doing any more substances for a little while, hopefully for forever.”

title: These young quarterbacks were supposed to break out. Now they’re hurt.
summary: The New York Giants’ Jaxson Dart on Monday became the latest upstart QB to be sidelined with an injury, joining the Bears’ Caleb Williams and the Commanders’ Jayden Daniels as signal callers who had to leave the field early in Week 2.
story: The New York Giants were one of the NFL’s pleasant surprises in Week 1, beginning the John Harbaugh era with an impressive win over the Dallas Cowboys thanks in large part to the play of second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart.

The Giants’ dreams of a turnaround season quickly hit a roadblock on Monday, however, as Dart became the latest upstart QB to be sidelined with an injury. Only two weeks into the NFL season, the game’s young stars are seeing their seasons upended due to varying degrees of injuries.

Dart joined the Chicago Bears’ Caleb Williams and the Washington Commanders’ Jayden Daniels as signal callers who had to leave the field early in Week 2. That trio joined a list of sidelined quarterbacks that also includes the Minnesota Vikings’ Kyler Murray and the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks’ Sam Darnold.
All five of those players are former first-round draft picks — and all are under the age of 30.

Dart left in the first quarter of New York’s 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. On a third-and-8 pass attempt, Dart was sandwiched by multiple players as the pocket collapsed around him, and he took a substantial hit to his left knee from a Rams linebacker.
Dart limped off the field and was taken back to the locker room. After initially being ruled questionable to return, he was ruled out for good in the second half.
“He’s going to be OK,” Giants general manager Joe Schoen told ESPN’s Laura Rutledge during the “Monday Night Football” broadcast, adding that Dart would undergo X-rays at the stadium.
Dart’s hard-charging play style raised eyebrows during his rookie season, when he missed time due to a concussion but seemingly refused to tone down his aggressiveness when he returned.
During the preseason, Dart even expressed confusion at why he so often is required to enter the blue medical tent on the sidelines.

“I really respect the rules, and the thought behind, you know, the NFL has of keeping players healthy and reviewing things,” Dart said in August after a big hit required he undergo a mandatory medical evaluation. “But at the same time, I’m still puzzled by just feeling like every time that I get hit, you know, I just find my way in there.”
Dart’s injury Monday, though, came on a relatively routine pass play, highlighting how no quarterback is ever truly safe.

The same can be said of the Commanders’ Daniels, who dislocated his left elbow while trying to regain his balance after he was tripped by one of his own lineman in a 37-20 loss to the Cowboys. Daniels, the 2024 Offensive Rookie of the Year, dislocated the same elbow last season, in which he appeared in only seven games due to multiple injuries.
“It sucks for him,” Washington coach Dan Quinn told reporters Monday. “I know how much these guys put into it. So, when there are setbacks like this, you just want to stand by them.”

A little before Daniels’ exit, the Bears’ Williams was carted off the field with a hamstring strain in a 9-3 loss to the Vikings. While Williams’ emotional exit from the game quickly became a social media meme, it also cut short what had been an exciting start to the season. Chicago was coming off a Week 1 in which it had scored 59 points.
“He’s right now working through every avenue that he’s got available to get back on track here. We’ll see what that looks like,” Bears coach Ben Johnson told reporters Monday.
Johnson added that Williams has an ability to recover quickly, and his injury is considered week-to-week.
While the Bears, Giants and the Commanders all lost after their starters went down, their seasons are far from over.
The Vikings lost Murray in Week 1 but still managed a 2-0 start to the season with Carson Wentz at the helm. And now Murray is expected to start in Week 3 after recovering from a concussion.

The Seahawks are also 2-0 with Drew Lock playing in place of Darnold, and even exploded for 31 points on Sunday. Darnold is expected to return to practice this week, though his starting status is up in the air.
For now, the Bears will turn to Tyler Bagent, the Giants to Jameis Winston, and the Commanders to Marcus Mariota as the three clubs try to keep their seasons afloat without their young leaders.

And Dart, Williams and Daniels — all three of whom have flashed potential to not only be great players but stewards for the league because of their exciting style of play — will have to wait a little longer to cement their star turns.

title: Climate scientists fired by Trump step in to fill U.S. report gap
summary: More than a year after the Trump administration dismissed hundreds of scientists working on the National Climate Assessment, clouding the landmark publication’s future, many of those researchers and others released Tuesday the first installment of a special collection of climate change findings designed to fill the perceived gap left behind.
story: More than a year after the Trump administration dismissed hundreds of scientists working on the National Climate Assessment, clouding the landmark publication’s future, many of those researchers and others released Tuesday the first installment of a special collection of climate change findings designed to fill the perceived gap left behind.

The new research commentary, published in scientific journals operated by the American Geophysical Union and American Meteorological Society, is meant to be something of a roadmap for what new climate research scientists should pursue and highlight to the public. As part of the special collection, the two organizations plan to publish additional research studies that state and local groups could use to build their own climate assessments.

“Scientists working on climate change are continuing to do the work,” said Melissa Kenney, a lead author of the report and the director of research at the University of Minnesota’s Institute on the Environment. “We’re stepping in to ensure that we have the research that we need, and that that is going to be available when we’re working with our communities, with our states, and that it will be available if there are future U.S. national climate assessments.”

In April 2025, the Trump administration halted independent scientists’ work on the sixth national assessment — a congressionally mandated report that summarizes the effects of global climate change in the United States — telling hundreds of scientists who had volunteered to contribute that they were no longer needed. The administration also cut funding to the U.S. Global Change Research Program, whose staffers organized the report’s production. The USGCRP website is no longer online.

title: Trump to address the U.N. General Assembly as Iran war rumbles on
summary: President Donald Trump will deliver a speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York City on Tuesday.
story: President Donald Trump will deliver a speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York City on Tuesday.

U.N. Ambassador Mike Waltz told reporters that the remarks would highlight peace deals the president has worked on, U.S. actions in the Western Hemisphere and progress on Trump’s 20-point peace plan in Gaza. It will also touch on the “importance of ensuring that Iran never has a nuclear weapon,” Waltz said.
The American president traditionally addresses the General Assembly each year.

In 2025, Trump spoke for almost an hour, criticizing climate change and European immigration policies. But what grabbed headlines were mishaps before and during his appearance at the U.N., as the escalator carrying Trump and first lady Melania Trump abruptly stopped and then the teleprompter with Trump’s speech broke early on in his remarks and he was forced to improvise.

Trump at the time blamed the world body, insinuating intentional sabotage to humiliate him, while U.N. officials said the White House’s videographer “may have inadvertently triggered the safety function” on the escalator.

Trump’s remarks to the assembly this year come as the U.N.’s Human Rights Council found in a report last week “reasonable grounds to believe” that the U.S. had committed war crimes during “indiscriminate attacks” against an Iranian school and a residential area in February.

Trump is expected to meet with several world leaders this week on the sidelines of the U.N. gathering, including Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez. It will be Rodríguez’s first meeting with Trump since the U.S. captured then-Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, who are in a Brooklyn jail awaiting trial.

Trump is also expected to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has said the meeting “could change a lot,” adding that there “is diplomatic momentum” in a push for an energy truce with the Kremlin.
Last week, Trump signed into law a Russian sanctions bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C.

He also announced that the U.S. would take over military operations and have “permanent control over security” in Greenland, in a deal expected to be signed Tuesday with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark to try and end the tense standoff over the strategic Arctic territory.

The U.N. assembly comes as the Iran war is about to enter its eighth month. Trump is expected to meet with leaders of the Gulf Cooperation Council, which includes Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday. Senior U.S. officials said Iran will be a key topic of conversation at the assembly this year.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the U.N. on Wednesday. Trump told Fox News that he would “probably” be open to meeting with Pezeshkian, but did not announce any specifics.

title: No criminal charges in death of Nolan Wells, grand jury finds
summary: A grand jury will not pursue criminal charges in the death of Nolan Wells, the local district attorney said, forcefully rejecting months of speculation that race played a role in the death of the Mississippi teen this summer.
story: A grand jury will not pursue charges in the death of Nolan Wells, the local district attorney said Monday, forcefully rejecting months of speculation that race played a role in the death of the Mississippi teenager this summer.

District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath made the announcement in a video message, saying the grand jury returned a “no true bill,” meaning it did not find sufficient evidence to indict anyone with a crime. A partially redacted copy of the grand jury report was also posted to the DA’s Facebook page.

Wells, 18, was with friends celebrating July Fourth and was last seen on Horn Island, a barrier reef off Mississippi accessible only by boat. His body was found at the northwestern tip of the island July 6, his family’s lawyer said.

“There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan’s disappearance and death were racially motivated,” Myers McIlrath said. “Nolan’s friends loved Nolan, and Nolan loved them. Nolan chose to stay on the island that day, and there is not a scintilla of evidence to contradict that.”
The family’s lawyer, civil rights attorney Ben Crump, previously called into question whether race was a factor in Wells’ death, as it appeared Wells was one of a few Black people there that day.
On Monday, Myers McIlrath took direct aim at Crump and his team, saying they also previously informed her office that they’d found no evidence a crime had been committed against Wells.
“I’m not suggesting that a grieving mother police the rumors surrounding her child’s death,” the DA said. “What I am suggesting is that the Crump team knew better but did not do better.”
Crump in turn said a statement Tuesday, “This grand jury result leaves us with more questions than answers. Nolan’s family will not rest until we know what happened to him, and neither will we.”

“Mississippi’s own pathologist found two bruises on the back of this young man’s head ... An independent autopsy documented traces of blood and recent blunt force injuries to the back of Nolan’s head and his back. To this day, not one person has explained how they got there,” he added.
“We don’t know how Nolan died, and neither does the State of Mississippi. Mississippi must keep investigating,” Crump said. Wells’ parents are expected to make a public address later Tuesday.
State completes autopsy of Mississippi teen Nolan Wells
The grand jury issued 132 subpoenas and heard from 43 witnesses, and seven people were invited to testify before the panel, according to the partially redacted report.

It was made up of 23 grand jurors from a “cross section of citizens” from Jackson County between 27 and 68 of age, it said. Among them were 13 men and 10 women, including “12 Caucasians, five African Americans, one Asian, two Hispanics, two Native Americans and one individual who preferred ‘other,’” it said.

“The grand jury finds no credible evidence to support the public allegations that any persons who rode to or from Horn Island on July 4, 2026 ... engaged in any criminal conduct related to ​the death of Mr. Wells,” the report released by McIlrath’s office said.

Wells was last seen sometime in the afternoon of July 4. Friends told police that they had to leave early because their boat started taking on water but that Wells chose to stay and catch a ride back later with others.

The grand jury report found that it was common for people on Horn Island to “socialize on boats and in the water,” and that it was “not unusual or suspicious” for people to return from the island on different boats.

It concluded there was no evidence that Wells had any sort of physical altercation or argument with anyone the day he was last seen. It added “that the position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr. Wells’ body is consistent with drowning.”

Crump and Wells’ family have previously rejected notions that he drowned, saying he was athletic and a good swimmer. An independent autopsy commissioned by the family’s legal team found that the teenager’s cause and manner of death were “undetermined.”

The state’s chief medical examiner and a forensic pathologist retained by Wells’ family both “opined that the cause and manner of Mr. Wells’ death is undetermined and that drowning is a diagnosis of exclusion,” according to the grand jury report. It noted, however, that neither has ruled out accidental drowning as a cause.
Wells’ funeral July 20 attracted hundreds of people.

“Your absence has left an emptiness that can never truly be filled,” his mother, Christine Wells-Wonsley, said at the time. “In a world that can often feel dark, be like Nolan, be the light that brightens the lives of those around you.”

title: Flights resume after air traffic equipment failure snarls traffic in Newark, Philadelphia
summary: A major circuit blew at the Philadelphia facility that controls air traffic to Newark Liberty International, Teterboro and Philadelphia airports Monday — causing widespread delays and cancellations to thousands of flyers on the East Coast.
story: A major circuit blew at the Philadelphia facility that controls air traffic to Newark Liberty International, Teterboro and Philadelphia airports Monday — causing widespread delays and cancellations to thousands of flyers on the East Coast.

Dozens of planes were left idling for hours on runways across the region while the FAA scrambled to repair the issue affecting Philadelphia’s Terminal Radar Approach Control, or TRACON, facility that houses both a radar approach control room and an air traffic control tower.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said shortly after 5 p.m., some seven hours after the circuit blew, that the telecom lines had been repaired and all flights were resuming in the Northeast.
Delays would take time to clear, he said.

Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford said after the malfunction at TRACON that they tried to get the backup system up and discovered the backup line had been cut at a New Jersey construction site.
“That fiber break is probably 13 hours to repair,” Bedford warned. “It’s massive, I’m told. Meanwhile, we’ve got the new circuit ready to install now.”
Duffy said an Amtrak construction crew accidentally severed a fiber line in New Jersey, which caused a telecom outage and forced the FAA to pause Northeast flights.
“This incident underscores the need for additional funding to modernize aging infrastructure and prevent disruptions like this in the future,” Duffy wrote.
An Amtrak spokesperson told NBC that it was a New Jersey Transit contractor who accidentally cut the cable.

NJT said in a statement that a construction crew working between New Brunswick and North Brunswick “accidentally severed a fiber-optic cable” at 9:45 a.m. but indicated that it was working to determine if a Verizon crew might be at fault.
Verizon denied being at fault and placed blame with the NJT crew.

“Earlier today, construction crews for New Jersey Transit cut a Verizon fiber cable running adjacent to a rail line in New Jersey,” the company said in a statement. “Verizon’s facilities were fully functional up to that point.”
Initially, the FAA ordered ground stops at Newark Liberty International, Teterboro and Philadelphia airports.

Later, the ground stops were expanded to both LaGuardia and John F. Kennedy International airports in New York City, causing delays to hundreds of flights as many foreign leaders were flying in for the United Nations General Assembly.
The ground stop at Newark began around 10 a.m. after the stops at Teterboro and Philadelphia went into effect.
The result was departure delays of up to 150 minutes out of Newark and Philadelphia, according to the FAA’s website.

As of 6 p.m. ET, there were nearly 619 flights canceled at Newark airport and 197 flights canceled at Philadelphia, according to data from flightaware.com. Hundreds of additional flights were delayed at both airports.
One pilot appeared to be in the dark about what was causing the delays, according to an audio obtained by NBC News from ATC.com.
“What’s with the ungodly takeoff lines,” a pilot asked the air traffic control tower in Philadelphia at 11:45 a.m., according to the ATC.com audio.
“Equipment issues,” a controller replied.
“Is that expected to continue?” the pilot asked.
“No clue,” the controller said.
This is one of the heaviest air travel corridors in the country, and last year an equipment malfunction left about a dozen planes flying blind for 90 seconds in the crowded skies over New Jersey.
Duffy insisted at the time that there was never any danger of planes colliding during that brief communications breakdown.

title: Tourists get rescued from Oregon’s Lost Boy Beach after spelling ‘SOS’ with driftwood
summary: A group of tourists looking for a photo opportunity ended up stranded on the secluded Lost Boy Beach in Tillamook, Oregon, after the tide blocked their way out.
story: A group of tourists looking for a photo opportunity ended up stranded on a secluded beach in Tillamook, Oregon, after the tide blocked their way out, officials said Monday.

Volunteer firefighters and rescue teams responded to a 911 call about three people stranded on Lost Boy Beach on Wednesday afternoon, according to Netarts-Oceanside Fire District Chief Jeff McBrayer. Officials were concerned that the the tourists would be at risk for hypothermia due to the winds and temperature.

“Typically, we would wait until low tide, but that would have been late at night,” McBrayer told NBC News. “Our water rescue team used a rope system to access the victims, placed them in life vests and assisted them through the surf to safety.”
McBrayer did not identify the individuals but described them as “two males, one female” in their 20s. They were evaluated for injuries, but McBrayer said they only had “minor scrapes and bumps.”
Photos of the rescue posted to the Netarts-Oceanside Fire District’s Facebook page showed that the group wrote “SOS” on the beach out of what appears to be driftwood.

Lost Boy Beach is a remote area only accessible by crossing a sea cave or climbing down rough rocks, according to the Oregonian. An incoming tide can prevent anyone on the beach from leaving, the newspaper reported.

The tourists told authorities they were out on the beach seeking a photo opportunity, McBrayer said. He noted that his office has seen an uptick in visitors seeking to make videos to post on social media platforms like TikTok, but he does not know if that is related. He urged that tourists should be aware of the dangerous cliff sides in the area while they are visiting.

McBrayer also warned that the region is expecting higher tides in the months to come given that this is an El Niño year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration warned in May that El Niño, a climate pattern that brings warmer temperatures to the Pacific Ocean, could come with higher tides and coastal flooding in the fall and winter.
“We would encourage all visitors to utilize a tide app on their phones and talk to locals before trying to access dangerous areas on the coast,” McBrayer said.

title: Iowa GOP Senate candidate calls for Iran war to end despite voting to let Trump continue it
summary: Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, has voted against House resolutions directing President Donald Trump to halt the war with Iran six times, including as recently as last week.
story: Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, has voted against House resolutions directing President Donald Trump to halt the war with Iran six times, including as recently as last week.
But on Monday, the Republican Senate candidate called for an “immediate end” to the conflict.

“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Hinson wrote on X, calling for measures like suspending the gas tax, pausing diesel exports and replenishing the highway trust fund to provide relief from high costs.
“These actions to lower costs are needed ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end,” she said.
It drew a quick response from her Democratic opponent, Josh Turek, who also pointed to a seventh vote by Hinson against ending U.S. hostilities in Lebanon as part of the conflict in the Middle East.
In a reply to Hinson, Turek wrote on X, “it’s easy to send a tweet but when you had the chance to vote to end this war, you chose not to.”

“You voted seven times to continue it, including just last week. It’s time to actually end the forever wars and put Iowa and Iowans first,” Turek continued. “Glad you’re finally following my lead after waffling on the proposals I put forward last week to address the rising costs of the war in Iran.”

Last month, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter shifted its Iowa Senate race rating from “lean Republican” to “toss-up.” Trump won the state in the last three presidential elections, and Democrats haven’t won a Senate race there since 2008.
Hinson’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment about her prior votes against the Iran war powers measures in the House.

The latest resolution passed the House 220-204 last Tuesday, with seven Republicans joining all Democrats present in supporting it. Among those seven were Reps. Zach Nunn and Marianette Miller-Meeks of Iowa, who had previously opposed such measures but changed their position.
Both are running for re-election in battleground House districts. The Cook Political Report rates their races as “toss-ups.”

Hinson, a three-term congresswoman, has been increasingly characterizing herself as “bipartisan” and slowly distancing herself from the Trump administration as polls show voters disapprove of the president’s handling of the war and the economy. Her messaging and votes highlight the difficult balance of turning out Trump’s strongest supporters while appealing to the growing number of voters who have soured on him.

Last month, Hinson objected to his proposal to import more foreign beef. Last week, when Vice President JD Vance went to Council Bluffs, Iowa, to rally for Republicans, Hinson did not attend, citing a scheduling conflict.

“I want to make a shoutout to an amazing public servant,” Vance said in his remarks. “I know she couldn’t be here today, but are we going to elect Ashley Hinson the next United States senator from the great state of Iowa?”
Meanwhile, another Midwest Republican Senate candidate running in a tough race on Tuesday said the Iran war must end.
Former Rep. Mike Rogers said in a video released on social media that “the war with Iran needs to end and end quickly.”
“When it does, energy costs will plummet,” Rogers said. “But Michigan families can’t afford to wait for that to happen.”
Similar to Hinson, Rogers said he supported suspending the state and federal gas tax and a temporary embargo on American diesel exports.
In response, Rogers’ Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed said on X, “You’ve spent your entire campaign supporting the war in Iran. Liar, coward, fraud.”

title: What Princess Diana Said About King Charles, from Their Marriage to Their Children
summary: Read what Princess Diana had to say about her marriage to Prince Charles, who became King Charles.
story: To the outside world, Princess Diana and then-Prince Charles seemed to have a fairytale relationship. But over time, royal watchers discovered that there was a great deal of turmoil in the couple’s marriage.

The future king first met his bride-to-be in 1977. At the time, Diana was 16 years old and Charles was nearly 13 years her senior. In 1980, the duo began dating then got engaged in February 1981. Five months later, they said “I do” in a televised wedding ceremony.
The royal couple soon started a family and welcomed their first child, a son named William, in 1982, followed by a second son named Harry in 1984.

The couple’s seemingly picturesque life was filled with turmoil behind the scenes and they went on to separate in 1992. By 1995, Queen Elizabeth II recommended that they end their marriage for good, and the divorce was finalized in August 1996.

Before her death in a car accident in 1997, Diana spoke candidly about her relationship with Charles on several occasions, most notably in a series of recordings for a biography titled, “Diana: Her True Story.”
Now, the princess’s brother, Charles Spencer, is giving an intimate look at his sister’s life in his new memoir, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister.”
Before the book is released on Sept. 22, we’re taking a look back at what Diana said about her marriage to Charles and her life as a mother of two princes.
On the wedding:

Charles and Diana became husband and wife on July 29, 1981. The couple exchanged vows at St. Paul’s Cathedral in London in a televised wedding ceremony. Per the BBC, the broadcast was viewed by 750 million in 74 countries.
A 2017 National Geographic documentary titled “Diana: In Her Own Words” used audio from a series of interviews Diana participated in for her biography, “Diana: Her True Story.”
In the documentary, Diana described the feeling of bliss she experienced on her wedding day.

“I remember being so in love with my husband that I couldn’t take my eyes off him. I just absolutely thought I was the luckiest girl in the world and you know, he was going to look after me,” she said.
However, the day was largely overshadowed by feelings of sadness. Diana said she “cried a lot” after her wedding rehearsal earlier in the week because “the tension suddenly hit me.”
Diana went on to describe her wedding as “the worst day of my life.”
“I don’t think I was happy,” she recalled in a recording.
“I never tried to call it off in the sense of really doing that, but I think (it was) the worst day of my life,” she continued.
As she was walking down the aisle, Diana said she spotted Camilla Parker Bowles, one of Charles’ former flames.

According to Penny Junor’s biography of Camilla, “The Duchess: The Untold Story,” the future king was heartbroken when she married another man in 1973. Flash forward to 1978, and the former couple were still close friends. Junor’s book claims that Charles and Camilla even rekindled their romance briefly in “1978 or early 1979.”
While recalling the moment she spotted Camilla on her wedding day, Diana said, “And I thought, ‘Well, there we are. That’s it. Let’s hope that’s all over with,’” she said.
Per Jonathan Dimbleby’s authorized biography of Charles, the future king once again rekindled his romance with Camilla in 1986, while both were still married to other people.
In 1995, Camilla and her husband got divorced. Charles and Diana made their divorce official the following year. Charles and Camilla later got engaged and married in 2005.
On their honeymoon:
After their wedding, the newlyweds embarked on a cruise around the Mediterranean on a royal yacht then spent time in Scotland.
In 2026, a letter Diana wrote after her wedding went up for auction. Per The Telegraph, the letter was sent to her former classmate Katherine Hanbury.

“We had a blissful honeymoon with endless sun and luckily calm seas… we are now up in Scotland until the end of October, which is a big treat for us — I adore being outside all day & hate London!” the princess wrote.
In the letter, which was written two months after her wedding, Diana wrote that it was “wonderful being married” and described it to “a case of playing with grown ups.”

In 1992, biographer Andrew Morton published a biography titled “Diana: Her True Story.” Per People, the author asked one of Diana’s close friends to interview Diana then used those recordings to write the book.
In the biography, Morton described the pain Diana felt on her honeymoon as she became fixated on her husband’s connection with Camilla Parker Bowles.
“At night, I dreamt of Camilla the whole time,” she said, adding that she was “obsessed by Camilla totally.”
Per People, Diana saw two photos of Camilla fall out of her husband’s diary during their honeymoon. Before their wedding, Diana also found a “goodbye” bracelet the groom was going to give Camilla.
In his biography of Diana, Morton described how Charles and Diana had a fight during their honeymoon when he wore a pair of cufflinks Camilla had given him.

“Cufflinks arrive on his wrists — two ‘C’s entwined like the Chanel ‘C’s. Got it in one; knew exactly. ‘Camilla gave you those, didn’t she?’” Diana said. “He said, ‘Yes, so what’s wrong? They’re a present from a friend.’ And, boy, did we have a row.”
In the documentary “Diana: In Her Own Words,” Diana recalled how her husband brought eight books with him on vacation.
“We were never on our own,” she said.
The princess also discussed her struggles with disordered eating, which was ever-present during her honeymoon.
“By then the bulimia was appalling,” she said. “It was four times a day on the yacht.”
On their kids:
During their marriage, Diana and Charles welcomed two sons named William and Harry.
In 1995, Diana sat down with BBC Panorama for a controversial interview with journalist Martin Bashir. During their chat, she said that she always wanted to be a mother.

“I came from a family where there were four of us, so we had enormous fun there,” she said. “And then William and Harry arrived — fortunately two boys, it would have been a little tricky if it had been two girls — but that in itself brings the responsibilities of bringing them up, William’s future being as it is, and Harry like a form of a back-up in that aspect.”
Diana discussed her “difficult pregnancy” and said she also experienced “post-natal depression” after delivering William.

“I received a great deal of treatment, but I knew in myself that actually what I needed was space and time to adapt to all the different roles that had come my way. I knew I could do it, but I needed people to be patient and give me the space to do it,” she said.
In the documentary “Diana: In Her Own Words,” Diana described the period between welcoming William and Harry as “total darkness” as the troubles in her marriage intensified.
“I can’t remember much. I’ve blotted it out. It was such pain,” she said.
However, the princess recalled how she and Charles were “very, very close” to each other during the six weeks before Harry was born, saying they were “the closest we’ve ever been.”
“And then as suddenly as Harry was born, it just went bang, our marriage. The whole thing went down the drain,” she said.
Diana added that Charles wanted a daughter, so she didn’t tell her husband when she found out that she was expecting another son.
“He wanted two children and he wanted a girl,” she said.

During her interview with Bashir, Diana said her biggest hope for her sons was that they develop “an understanding of people’s emotions, people’s insecurities, people’s distress, and people’s hopes and dreams.”
Diana described William as a “deep thinker” in the interview and described Harry as “complete joy” in the documentary “Diana: In Her Own Words.”
On their divorce:

Diana and Charles separated in 1992 and ultimately divorced in 1996. According to Diana, factors that led to the divorce included “pressure of the media” and adultery. Charles admitted to being unfaithful in a 1994 interview. She also described depression and developed an eating disorder during her marriage, she told Bashir.
Speaking to Bashir, Diana said her own parents’ divorce made her want to “make it work” even more.
“I desperately wanted it to work, I desperately loved my husband and I wanted to share everything together, and I thought that we were a very good team,” she said.
When Diana learned that news of Charles’ infidelity was going public, she was concerned about how it would affect her sons.

“William asked me what had been going on, and could I answer his questions, which I did. He said, was that the reason why our marriage had broken up? And I said, well, there were three of us in this marriage, and the pressure of the media was another factor, so the two together were very difficult. But although I still loved Papa I couldn’t live under the same roof as him, and likewise with him,” she continued.
Diana told Bashir that she took responsibility for the end of the marriage: “We both made mistakes.” For example, she admitted to infidelity on her own end in the interview.

“I take full responsibility, I take some responsibility that our marriage went the way it did. I’ll take half of it, but I won’t take any more than that, because it takes two to get in this situation,” she said.

title: Presley Gerber Shared Mental Health, Addiction Struggles Before Death: ‘I’ve Had a Lot of Time to Look Into Myself’
summary: Presley Gerber shared his struggle with mental health and addiction before his death in a rehab facility at 27. What he said about drugs, alcohol, depression.
story: Presley Gerber was open about his struggles with mental health and substance use before his death at 27.
The son of model Cindy Crawford and businessman Rande Gerber passed away Sunday.
“The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time,” a statement on behalf of his family noted.
Gerber, who began modeling as a teen, once called dealing with mental health issues a “24/7 job” and posted candid videos he called “Mental Health Mondays” on his Instagram page.
How Did Presley Gerber Die? What We Know
Gerber died at a “rehab facility,” according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner.
No cause of death was given, but an exam of his body has been scheduled, the website entry notes.
Police responded to a report of a possible overdose at about 9:35 a.m. on Sunday, Sept. 20, and found “an adult male who was deceased,” the Santa Monica Police Department said in a statement.
Detectives are investigating the death “as a suspected overdose. At this time, there is no indication of foul play,” the statement noted.

A law enforcement source told NBC News that he was found unresponsive at the rehab facility in Los Angeles on Sunday morning. He had checked into the facility at 10 p.m. the night before. The sourced added that he had likely been dead for some time when he was found in the room where he was sleeping.
He Spoke About Mental Health at an Event a Few Months Before His Death

In June, Gerber appeared with his parents at an event in Malibu, California, where he took part in a “candid panel discussion about mental health,” People magazine reported. It was his last public appearance.
“The most free I felt was when I was finally honest with myself,” he told the audience.
The model also offered advice about boosting mental health: “Move your body regardless of how you’re feeling. Get outside. Get some sun,” he said. “If you don’t feel like moving, lay on the grass.”

In December 2025, Presley spoke about his struggles in a since-deleted video on Instagram, revealing he’d largely given up drinking in recent years, noting that alcohol was “no longer serving” him, E! News reported.

He said he was taking various medications including Valium — the brand name for diazepam, which is used to relieve anxiety and control agitation caused by alcohol withdrawal — and buprenorphine, a medication to treat opioid use disorder, according to E! News.

He added he was also taking Xanax, the brand name for alprazolam, which is used to treat anxiety and panic disorders, for “when the panic attacks are really, really bad,” but was seeking more direction about his dosages.

“Every psychiatrist I’ve had — and I’ve had, like, 15 — they’re all like, ‘Here’s 20 medications,’” Gerber said. “‘Take this if you feel like this, take this as needed.’ And I’m like, ‘No, don’t give me that much leeway. I need some direction.’”
He Was a Mental Health Advocate
In a 2023 podcast, he said he struggled with mental health and depression, and wanted to help others dealing with similar issues.
“Whether I help one person or a 100 people get out of that place that I was in at one point in my life, that’s all I need to do,” Gerber said.
“I’ve had a lot of time to look into myself and learn about myself with therapists.”
Mental health is “such a big part of my life,” he added, calling his focus on it a “24/7 job” and noting “there’s no judgement.”

“I’ve seen a lot of stuff and I’ve learned a lot of things, and what I hope I can do is have made the mistakes for some other people so they don’t have to make the same mistakes that I made,” he said.
He Tried Ibogaine
In a video he posted on Instagram in March, Gerber was seen in Cancun, Mexico, taking part in what he describes as a “Pre Ibogaine Flood Dose — quiet moment before everything changed.”

“I was absolutely terrified,” he writes in the caption. “Letting go of control didn’t come easy, but I trusted there was something bigger than me guiding it. I knew why i was there. I faced what I had been running from, and somewhere in all of it, i started finding my way back to myself.”

Ibogaine, a psychoactive compound found in the root of Tabernanthe iboga, a shrub native to Central Africa, has been studied for its potential in treating opioid and alcohol addiction, and other substance use disorders, according to the University of Virginia Division of Medical Toxicology.
It has hallucinogenic properties, and may prevent cravings and withdrawal.
Sister Kaia Gerber Spoke About His Addiction Struggles in a Recent Interview
After Gerber posted the candid video about his struggles in December, his younger sister, Kaia, praised his honesty and vulnerability.

“My parents for most of our lives were very, very private and didn’t share anything — and now we have this absolute teacher, my brother, who says, ‘I’m gonna be very human for everyone.’ There’s only so much you can hide from the world. And trying to put a lid on something just makes the person feel like you’re ashamed of them,” she told Vogue.
The outlet noted that he had a “decade-long struggle with drug addiction.”

title: ‘The Voice’ Season 30 Kicks Off With a 4-Chair Turn, New Rule and Poking Fun at Riley Green
summary: “The Voice” Season 30 kicked off on Sept. 21 with singers joining either Team Adam Levine, Kelly Clarkson, Queen Latifah or Riley Green.
story: “The Voice” is back and the red chairs are turning.

Season 30 of the NBC singing competition show kicked off on Monday, Sept. 21 with a two-hour premiere. Returning coaches Adam Levine, who won the previous season, and Kelly Clarkson welcomed Queen Latifah and Riley Green to the show as the Blind Auditions began.
Queen Latifah called being a part of “The Voice” a “pinch-me moment,” while the country star made his presence known by using a duck call.

During the first episode, the “First In Button” was introduced, which means that whichever coach turns first in a multi-chair turn has the chance to claim an artist before the artist’s final decision. They can only use this button once. Additionally, there are no blocks this season.

Host Carson Daly also shared that this season they will be tracking which contestants get the most likes and views on “The Voice”s TikTok and the “finalist with the most overall likes and shares will be named the TikTok artist of the season.”

A country-singing sister duo got the first four-chair turn of the night, and Queen Latifah used her “First In Button” to steal a singer from Kelly and Riley.
The “Worst Way” crooner also used his adorable pup Carl to convince a young star to join his team, but unfortunately it did not work.
