title: Did Lizzie Borden Ever Have A Romance With Maid Bridget Sullivan? An Expert Unpacks the True Story Behind ‘Monster’ Season 4
summary: Did Lizzie Borden have an affair with her maid? What historian Cara Robertson said in an interview.
story: In Netflix’s “Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story,” domestic servant Bridget Sullivan is portrayed as a seductive manipulator who plays a substantial role in the dynamics that lead to Lizzie Borden’s infamous trial for the gruesome Aug. 1982 murders of her father and stepmother.
But the sensational nature of the series has viewers wondering if the maid, played by actor Vicky Krieps, was truly the figure who was stirring the pot in the real-life Borden family all along.

It turns out, the true story of Bridget Sullivan was far less salacious. And though the season, which was released on Sept. 17, depicts her as entangled in a romance with Lizzie Borden herself, experts and historical accounts show that the pair had a professional relationship — one that never crossed into the realm of lust.

As Cara Robertson — author of the book “The Trial of Lizzie Borden,” which is largely considered the definitive account of the case — tells TODAY.com, it “sounds as if they want to make this a sexy story and it just isn’t.”
How is Bridget Sullivan Portrayed in ‘Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story?’
Bridget makes her mark not long into the first episode of the series.

After the Borden household goes through a slew of maids, Bridget interviews with the family and immediately impresses matriarch Abby Borden, Lizzie’s harsh, hard-to-please stepmother, with the way in which she is able to remove a stubborn blood stain from a prized fainting couch. Patriarch Andrew Borden is also struck by Bridget’s presence, drawn to her lack of queasiness around blood — something that’s important to him as a woodworker who builds coffins for a living.

But perhaps the person most captivated by Bridget is Lizzie herself, particularly after the new maid takes a special interest in her, introducing Lizzie to some more risqué things, including a hand-cranked vibrator. Bridget also attempts to ingratiate herself with Lizzie but emphasizing Abby’s poor treatment of her.
“I don’t know why she belittles you like that,” Bridget says to Lizzie in the first episode, entitled “Bloodbath.” “She’s the most cruel woman I’ve ever seen.”
Though Lizzie appears to be more sympathetic to her stepmother’s temper, Bridget’s tactic works. And before long, there are secret bedroom visits and intimate meetings between the two.

Their sexual tension-filled bond is cemented by the end of the premiere episode when the two share a bath of cherry juice, inspired by Elizabeth Báthory, a 16th century Hungarian countess who is said to have bathed in the blood of young women to preserve her beauty, though Bathory’s infamous blood baths are likely myth rather than truth.
Earlier in the episode, it is Bridget who gifts the story of Báthory to Lizzie.
What Was The Real-Life Bridget Sullivan Really Like?
The real-life Bridget Sullivan was indeed a maid for the family. But aside from that detail, the similarities between Sullivan and her “Monster” character are few and far between.

Sullivan, who hailed from Ireland, worked for the Borden family for a number of years, starting in 1889, according to the Lizzie Borden House. However, according to Robertson’s book, she was not always happy with her employment, telling an officer that she had attempted to leave the position on multiple occasions.

As the book points out, most of the members of the Borden family did not bother to learn Sullivan’s name, calling her “Maggie,” simply because that was the name of the family’s domestic servant before her.
Sullivan also wasn’t particularly entrenched in the family’s drama, Robertson says.
“Bridget was an observer of the family tensions.  She lived in the house and negotiated the dynamics,” the author says.
Nor is there any evidence that Bridget was a master manipulator, she adds.

The 25-year-old Sullivan did end up becoming a key witness in the trial, as she was in the home at the time of the murders. Though Sullivan testified over the course of two days, she was ruled out as a possible suspect.
So Did Bridget Ever Have A Romance With Lizzie?

Over the decades, many have attempted to romantically link Lizzie Borden with Sullivan, especially because the former was never married and considered a spinster for the time. But the truth is that there’s just never been any evidence that points toward a steamy affair between the two. It was all just strictly professional, Robertson explains.

“This is simply a newer version of a longstanding desire to give Lizzie a fictional romance,” Robertson says. “It’s as if writers and adapters of the story can’t make their stories work without inserting a love interest.”
What’s more, the real-life Sullivan had a rather sunny view of Abby Borden. Robertson says that Abby Borden was the only person in the household who bothered to call her by her real name.
“We really don’t know much about her relationship with Abby,” Robertson says. “Bridget spoke positively of her after her death, calling her ‘a lovely woman.’”

Bridget Sullivan herself did eventually marry. After the murders, she eventually found her way to Anaconda, Montana where she tied the knot with laborer and fellow Irish immigrant John Sullivan, according to the Lizzie Borden House. With the middle-class living that John Sullivan was able to provide, Bridget Sullivan left behind her work as a domestic servant. She refused, however, to speak of the murders ever again.

title: ‘Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story’ Reviews: Here’s What Critics Are Saying
summary: “The Lizzie Borden Story,” the latest installment in Ryan Murphy’s “Monster” series is raising a few eyebrows. Find out if critics think it’s worth the watch.
story: Ryan Murphy has just released “The Lizzie Borden Story,” the latest installment in his “Monster” franchise.

Like past seasons, which include “The Jeffrey Dahmer Story,” “The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story” and “The Ed Gein Story,” Murphy’s latest offering is a true-crime horror series. This time it focuses on a century-old murder.

Starring Ella Beatty, Vicky Krieps, Rebecca Hall and Charlie Hunnam, the 8-episode series is based on the real-life killings of Abby and Andrew Borden. Residents of the Massachusetts city of Fall River, the Bordens were violently bludgeoned to death in their home in 1892, with each receiving multiple blows with a hatchet.

Their 32-year-old daughter, Lizzie, was arrested and charged in the crime. However, after a months’ long trial, Lizzie Borden was acquitted of the killings. While it’s been 134 years since the murders, it still remains one of the most famous unsolved crimes in American history.

Murphy, in collaboration with Ian Brennan and director Matt Winkler, brings the controversial crime story to the small screen in his newest Netflix series. And much like his previous offerings, “Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story” has been met with both praise and pans.
If you’re wondering if the crime thriller is worth the watch, see below for a roundup of the latest reviews and decide for yourself.
Aramide Tinubu, TV critic, writes in Variety that the new series “has a playful, vibrant tone” and offers “something refreshing and wholly unique to the ‘Monster’ canon.”

Tinubu also writes that Murphy’s take on the Lizzie Borden story is a “highly watchable depiction of one of the most gruesome crimes in American history,” while acknowledging that the storyline “bends and twists the truth” of what actually transpired in 1892.
The Variety critic also writes that parts of the series highlight “the obsession with women’s appearances across time” in a way that adds to the show’s “fun campiness and gothic nature.”
She concludes that “The Lizzie Borden Story” is a reminder “that the last person anyone should underestimate is a woman, especially one clamoring for even a small slice of freedom.”
The Guardian
Lucy Mangan, TV critic, is less flattering in her write up for The Guardian, calling the latest “Monster” installment an “utterly bonkers, blood-soaked, borderline-fetishistic fever dream.”
In her review, Mangan likens the creative process behind the series to “the gleeful disgust of a roomful of adolescent boys being taught about the female reproductive system in PSHE.”

While the real-life Borden murders are a deeply complex mystery, The Guardian review suggests that “The Lizzie Borden Story” offers a much simpler message: “Women be crazy! Especially women who menstruate!”
Mangan does acknowledge that the show is stylish with a “Wes Anderson feel at times” and that it’s “full of great performances.”

But ultimately, Mangan writes that “The Lizzie Borden Story” feels as though it was created by “a bunch of boys on a dare who should have been called back after class and made to get down to some real work.”
The Hollywood Reporter
According to The Hollywood Reporter, the Lizzie Borden drama is nothing short of “faux-feminist nonsense.”

Television critic Angie Han writes that Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan desperately try to draw “anything meaningful out of Borden’s saga” and do so “with all the finesse of a college freshman trying to crank out a 15-page term paper in the two hours before deadline.”
Of actors Hall and Hunnam, Han writes, “There’s zero nuance to their performances, and also nothing unique about them to make them memorable.”

With the murder mystery seemingly solved early on in the series, Han writes that “The Lizzie Borden Story” struggles with “having eight hours’ worth of content to fill” and that the show “flails about for a number of stalling tactics, none of them particularly satisfying.”
The Wrap
“Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan have never been particularly interested in letting a little historical fact get in the way of a good story,” notes movie and TV critic Matthew Creith.

In his review for The Wrap, Creith writes that the creative team behind “The Lizzie Borden Story” takes one of America’s most infamous murder cases and “gleefully blends it into gothic horror, sexual melodrama and blood-soaked camp” and that the series is “hardly a conventional retelling of the Lizzie Borden case.”
So much so, Creith writes “calling it ‘The Lizzie Borden Story’ feels almost deliberately misleading.”
The “poisoned meals, bloody corpses, severed heads” and “axes flying around” make the show “frequently hilarious, even when it isn’t necessarily trying to be,” observes Creith.
Beyond that, he also faults “The Lizzie Borden Story” for randoming including the addition of real-life serial killer Aileen Wuornos “for absolutely no reason.”
Creith does, however, laud Sarah Paulson’s performance as Wuornos, calling it “manic, twitchy and unnerving and that it captures Wuornos “without making the character another true-crime caricature.”
He also notes Rebecca Hall’s “shrill, vicious” portrayal of Abby Borden, calling it a “scene-stealer” in the series.

In sum, “The Lizzie Borden Story” is one where “patriarchal cruelty meets female revenge, with history merely the jumping-off point,” he writes before concluding, “If that sounds like a mess … it is.”
Rotten Tomatoes
Finally, if you head over to Rotten Tomatoes, you’ll find that the series currently has a 50% on its “Tomatometer,” which averages critics’ reviews into a single median score.
On the site’s “Popcornmeter,” which measures audience reviews, “The Lizzie Borden Story” currently sits at 26%.

title: Who Is Rachel Danis? About Patrick Clancy’s Wife, Who Is Speaking Out in a New Interview
summary: Patrick Clancy and his wife Rachel Danis are speaking out following the conclusion of his ex-wife Lindsay Clancy’s triple murder trial, which ended in a mistrial.
story: Patrick Clancy and his wife Rachel Danis spoke out following the conclusion of his ex-wife Lindsay Clancy’s triple murder trial, which ended in a mistrial. The two married after Patrick Clancy divorced Lindsay Clancy following the 2023 killings.
So who is Rachel Danis, the woman who is now Patrick Clancy’s new wife?

Danis sat down alongside Patrick Clancy for his pre-taped appearance on CBS’ “60 Minutes,” which aired Sept. 20. The interview marked his first since a judge earlier this month declared a mistrial when a jury — who had been tasked with determining whether Lindsay Clancy was criminally responsible for killing her three children — failed to reach a unanimous verdict.
In the interview, Danis shared that she met Patrick Clancy in a New York City run club in January 2024. They then grabbed coffee together.
“Pat pulls out his phone to pay and I noticed this adorable photo of children as the wallpaper,” she recalled. “And I just asked, ‘Who are those cuties?’ And Pat had said, ‘Those are my kids.’”
Danis said she inquired about where the children lived.
“And Pat said, ‘They died.’ And this is just at the cashier,” she shared.
Danis remembered having many follow-up questions but not being sure how to ask them.
The couple continued to get to know each other and tied the knot in April 2026.
Later in the sit-down, Danis spoke more about Patrick Clancy’s children. She said she tries to help him manage his grief while understanding she “can’t bring his kids back.”
“But if I can honor them and allow Pat to grieve but also just continue to honor them in the present, I guess that’s all I can do,” she continued.
The pair also confirmed that they are starting a family.
“I think every parent can agree you have different relationships with you kids, but they’re all your kids. I can’t wait to tell them about their brothers and sister,” Patrick Clancy said.

During the trial, which ended Sept. 4, the prosecution argued that Lindsay Clancy had intentionally and knowingly attacked her three children. Meanwhile, her defense did not dispute the fact that she had killed her children. But they argued that she is not criminally responsible for the murders, as she was consumed by the rare mental health condition postpartum psychosis.
Read on to learn what Danis has said about the case and what she shared about her relationship with Patrick Clancy.
Who Is Rachel Danis?

Danis is a New York-based fertility doctor. According to her professional page, she’s specifically a reproductive endocrinologist and infertility specialist at clinic RMA of New York. She’s also an assistant clinical professor at Mount Sinai’s Icahn School of Medicine.

Danis specializes in endometriosis, an often painful condition in which tissue similar to what typically lines the uterus ends up on other organs. She also specializes in ovulation induction, LGBTQIA family building and fertility preservation, according to her professional biography. At one point, she was awarded a grant to conduct a clinical trial using Orlissa, a drug that aims to help patients manage moderate to severe endometriosis pain.

According to her professional bio, she’s somewhat of a fitness aficionado outside of work, and can often be found in a bootcamp class or ballet class. She also enjoys baking and strolls through Central Park, according to the website.
How Did She Meet Patrick Clancy?
Danis, who married Patrick Clancy in April, shared in a newly released clip from the upcoming “60 Minutes” interview that she met Clancy in Manhattan’s Central Park.
“I was just a girl that met a guy running in Central Park on a really cold Saturday,” Danis said. “And I don’t think there’s anything wrong with that.”

Patrick Clancy, who divorced Lindsay Clancy following the 2023 killings, relocated to New York from the suburbs of Boston after the tragedy. By Oct. 2024, Clancy was living in what the New Yorker described in a feature as an apartment in Manhattan that resembled a “tidy bachelor pad,” which included a few keepsakes from his late children Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months. Clancy did not comment on his relationship status with Lindsay Clancy at the time, nor did he mention Danis.
Lindsay Clancy’s defense attorney Kevin Reddington confirmed in court that Patrick Clancy had remarried and is “trying to move on.”
How Was Danis Impacted During The Trial?

While Danis did not take the stand during the nearly six-week trial over the summer, Patrick Clancy spent two days testifying on the events that led up to the killings in addition to Lindsay Clancy’s deteriorating mental health prior to the tragedy.

However, Danis became a topic of conversation when conspiracies began to arise on social media from internet users who accused Patrick Clancy of killing his children. Others online have also accused the father of framing the defendant. And in the days that followed the trial, Danis and Patrick Clancy were frequently the subject of paparazzi photos in addition to harassment.
In the interview, Danis defended their marriage.
“I don’t understand how the story has been so twisted, but I would hope people know that Pat is, as I said before, the most selfless father and supportive partner,” she said.

Patrick Clancy and others involved in the case have made multiple attempts to shut down internet conspiracies. In a Sept. 9 interview with NBC News’ Laura Jarrett, Reddington called on people to stop spreading misinformation and attacking Patrick Clancy.
“His life has been turned upside down into a nightmare that he doesn’t deserve,” Reddington said. “Period. Full stop.”
The defense attorney added that he has “said it repeatedly, unequivocally, that there is absolutely no way that this guy deserves what he has been living (through).”

The day prior, Patrick Clancy’s attorneys also attempted to shut down the noise from conspiracy theorists. One of his attorneys, Howard Cooper, mentioned in a statement that law enforcement “has been notified” about the claims and that “every appropriate measure will be pursued to hold them accountable, including legally.”
“This campaign, now fueled by insatiable media coverage, remains at a fever pitch and has resulted in real life threats to his reputation, livelihood, and life,” Cooper said in the Sept. 8 statement.

title: Lucy Foley Revives Agatha Christie’s Miss Marple For the Character’s First Novel in 50 Years. Read the Prologue
summary: Sleuth Miss Marple, created by Agatha Christie, has once again found herself at the scene of a crime in Lucy Foley’s “Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel.” Read the prologue.
story: It is a truth universally acknowledged that a good story starts with a good first line. In TODAY’s “Cold Open,” authors tease their buzzy upcoming release by revealing and explaining its first line, paragraph or page.
After 50 years away, cunning and perceptive sleuth Miss Marple has once again found herself at the scene of a crime.

The elderly character at the center of many Agatha Christie whodunits is tasked with solving a new case in Lucy Foley’s latest mystery “Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel,” out Sept. 22. Christie is also listed as an author.

Set at a secluded resort in Switzerland, the Grand Alpine is practically cut off from the outside world, only accessible via a gondola ride during particular hours of the day. And it’s precisely there that the book begins. The prologue opens with the line:
The gondola rises silently through the bank of clouds into the frozen world at the top of the mountain.

Foley tells TODAY.com the eerie, chilling setting was the perfect place to make Miss Marple — who last appeared in a novel in Christie’s 1976 work “Sleeping Murder” — the “beating heart” of the story.

The bestselling British author behind “The Guest List” and “The Paris Apartment” grew up a fan of Christie, discovering one of her detective novels on a bookshelf in a cottage when she was just 12. She devoured more stories but she didn’t appreciate Miss Marple’s character, she recalls.
It wasn’t until she re-read some of Christie’s novels that she admired how the writer took an “underdog character” and made “her a master sleuth with a brain to rival Sherlock Holmes.”

“It was so clever, and it still feels radical even today,” Foley says. “I think we still have an issue with older women being perceived as invisible or less capable in some way. I still think she has something to teach us.”

In 2022, Foley was asked to contribute to a collection of 12 new Marple stories, alongside Leigh Bardugo, Ruth Ware, Jean Kwok and more. When she was approached again about the character, this time for a full-length novel, she jumped at the opportunity.

“In 2026, we need a new kind of superhero. We’re surrounded by these male egos and these men rewriting history to further their own ends. I love thinking, ‘What would Miss Marple make of them, and how would she thwart them?’” she says.

Still, she initially felt the pressure of doing the character justice. But once she had her premise — Miss Marple on a holiday to the Swiss Alps in the 1950s — she entered her creative bubble and started plotting the mystery.

“It felt like quite a haunted time in many ways because there was this long shadow of the Second World War. I wanted that to be something that I contrasted with the glamour,” she says of the setting of “Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel.”

She also knew how she wanted to structure the novel. Fans of Foley’s other books will know that the writer tells each chapter from a different character’s first person point of view. With Miss Marple, though, she decided readers wouldn’t hear the inner workings of the detective’s mind.

“I knew that I couldn’t have her perspective because that would feel like a real Christie anachronism,” she says, laughing. “Because I think the really interesting thing about Miss Marple is she’s quite enigmatic, and she doesn’t actually necessarily reveal a lot of herself.”

The character works best as an underestimated observer, Foley shares, and she wanted to keep her that way. She read, and re-read, Christie’s books to nail Miss Marple’s tone and mannerisms. She also watched the British television series.

“There were two things that I knew I had to get right for this book before I brought in any of my own sort of creative sensibilities, and those were the Christie plotting… (and) also Miss Marple. So I wanted to get her on the page as closely as I possibly could to Christie’s Miss Marple,” Foley says.
Beyond that, she says she had “some license” to bring in her own voice and style.
“I wanted it to be a book that was in conversation with the original Miss Marple,” Foley says. “They didn’t want to present it as a kind of Agatha Christie forgery.”
With those goals in mind, Foley plotted out the entire book before she started writing, a change to her usual process.

While Miss Marple isn’t mentioned in the prologue, she is quickly introduced in Chapter 1, which is told from the perspective of Diana Glass, described as “the help.” Diana meets Miss Marple and describes her as a “the perfect image of a little old lady — almost too perfect, in fact.”

“I wanted, through Diana’s eyes, a reader who’s familiar with Miss Marple to recognize this character that they know and love. But also a reader coming to her completely cold, not knowing much about her, to quite quickly get a sense of who she is through Diana’s perspective,” Foley says.
Readers then meet more characters who will all become suspects in the death of the unnamed person found in the gondola. Miss Marple must suss out the culprit before they commit their next crime.

“As a reader of murder mysteries, I love this sense of the past catching up with people and people not getting away with things when they shouldn’t,” Foley says. “But I also love this idea, chaos is then going to be resolved for you at the end. There’s a nice wrapping up and a nice sense of resolution. I think that can be quite soothing and satisfying in troubled times.”
It’s all set up in a prologue, which Foley says was the first scene she thought of when she started writing.
“The first scene that came to me was the gondola going up the mountain,” she says. “The set piece of someone getting into the gondola alive and well at the bottom, and being found dead at the top.”
Get a taste of the mystery below.
Read the Prologue of Lucy Foley’s ‘Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel’
The top of the Grand Alpine gondola
Swiss Alps, 1950

The gondola rises silently through the bank of clouds into the frozen world at the top of the mountain. It is a wonder of modern engineer-ing, gliding between stanchions drilled into ancient rock, the red lacquer of its body gaudy against the bleak palette of white and gray.

There’s someone in the gondola. One of the hotel guests, most likely, eager to make the first tracks of the day. Fresh snow fell last night, leaving a pristine covering of powder over the mountain and softening the glacier that sweeps down one side. In the early morning light, it gives off a nacreous glow. Faint bluish indentations on the surface whisper of hidden, lethal chasms beneath.

In the tiny cabin beside the lift the attendant stamps his feet in his boots, blows on his hands to keep warm. He’s looking forward to interacting with another human being, however briefly. It’s a lonely existence up here with only the eagles for company, the only sounds the otherworldly groaning and cracking of the glacial ice as it con-tinues its endless creep toward the town. He knows the fears of his ancestors, how they believed in malign mountain spirits and giants living among these peaks, why they shunned them as a place of dark magic. Sometimes—­ when the seracs fall with crashes that seem to echo infinitely among the surrounding rock, or when a winter storm crackles with purple lightning, or when the low growl of an avalanche sounds at a distance—­ he’s not completely sure he doesn’t believe in such things himself.

The shadowy figure in the gondola sits with their head thrown back against the rear window; perhaps in awestruck appreciation of the view. The mechanism grinds to a halt. The doors begin to open. The seated figure does not move.

The attendant peers through the cabin window. Are they asleep? Are they not intending to get out? Perhaps they’ve come up here for the sights and will simply stay put and travel back the way they’ve come. More snow is on the way, after all: a great deal of it.
And yet . . . there’s something odd. A peculiar stillness about the scene. The attendant feels that he is just as alone as he was before the gondola and its occupant emerged through the clouds.
Should he go and see?
He doesn’t want to see.
He’s struck by the sudden impulse (odd; he’s a good Swiss Prot-estant) to cross himself.

Just as he steps out of his cabin into the freezing air the gondola gives the mechanical shudder that locks it into the final position. This is when the seated figure falls, stiff and inert as a Dresden doll knocked from a mantelpiece, keeling face-­ first onto the metal floor of the cabin.
For a moment the attendant watches in horror. Then he springs into action. But he knows, even as he hastens along the ice-­ slick path, that it is no use. The gondola’s passenger is already dead.

title: Oil prices tumble to 2-week low on hopes for critical pipeline reopening and Iran diplomacy
summary: Oil prices fell sharply fell for a fifth straight trading session, reaching a two-week low on hopes of a renewed diplomatic push to end the Iran war and optimism over the reopening of a critical pipeline in Saudi Arabia.
story: Oil prices fell sharply fell for a fifth straight trading session, reaching a two-week low on hopes of a renewed diplomatic push to end the Iran war and optimism over the reopening of a critical pipeline in Saudi Arabia.
Brent crude oil briefly slipped below $98 per barrel while U.S. crude oil fell below $93 per barrel, their lowest prices since Sept. 8.
Prices first began sliding overnight on reports that Iran was offering to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days if the U.S. takes steps toward easing pressure on the country.
NBC News has not confirmed the reports. Iran’s semiofficial Fars news agency said that “Iranian sources have described these reports as unreliable and untrue,” without naming those sources.

It was the latest hint that there may be a window for Washington and Tehran to re-engage in their standoff over the Strait of Hormuz — a possibility that would be welcome relief for markets eager for the restoration of energy supplies from the Middle East.
President Donald Trump is holding a number of meetings with world leaders Tuesday at the United National General Assembly in New York City.

Trump signaled a willingness to meet with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, which had already soothed some market concerns. Asked about a potential meeting between the two leaders, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told NBC News, “I don’t think anything is scheduled at this point.”
Rubio added that the U.S. was “open to something like that,” though.

Since the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran war Feb. 28, vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has at times ground to a near halt. Over the course of the last week, daily traffic did not exceed 20 ships in a day, according to data from MarineTraffic.
Also fueling oil’s downward move Tuesday were reports about Saudi Arabia’s key east-west pipeline, which has effectively acted as a Strait of Hormuz workaround for oil exports.

On Sept. 11, the Saudi Energy Ministry said that the pipeline was shut after “multiple attacks” on it amid the escalating conflict with the Iran-backed Houthi rebels. Initially, experts worried that this closure could last months.

Reuters reported that the pipeline had already restarted, and could resume exports from a Red Sea port later in the day, citing three people familiar with the matter. Bloomberg News reported that Saudi Arabia was running tests on the pipeline with the hope of restarting it this week, citing multiple people familiar with the matter.
Saudi Aramco, which operates the pipeline, did not immediately respond to a request for comment from NBC News.

On NBC’s “TODAY,” Rubio said regarding prices, “if you look at the increases we’ve seen in just the last two weeks, the enormous majority of that increase is because the Houthi’s attacked a Saudi pipeline and the Saudis had to shut down that pipeline.”

“So there’s still oil in the system, but the markets are reacting to the expectation that there will not be as much Saudi oil in the future” as a result of the pipeline attack, Rubio added. “That is problem as well, which we are confronting here.”
Both oil benchmarks are elevated by more than 60% since the start of the year. So are retail gas prices, which as of Tuesday morning reached $4.47 per gallon. That’s up 50% since the Iran war began.
The price of diesel has also skyrocketed.

The national average hit a new all-time high of $6.52 per gallon Tuesday, up 82% since the start of year on a record run propelled in part by intensifying aerial attacks between Russia and Ukraine. Trump is set to hold talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday as he pushes for an energy truce.

Along with tumbling oil prices, bond yields also fell early Tuesday. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield, which heavily influences consumer borrowing rates, fell to as low as 4.92%, after reaching as high as 5.04% a week ago. That was its highest level since 2007.
The 30-year Treasury yield also dipped to as low as 5.25% Tuesday morning. Last week, it rose as high as 5.4%, a level it also last touched in 2007.
Global stocks rallied as well. The European-wide Stoxx 600 index rose more than 0.5%, as did Germany’s benchmark DAX and France CAC 40 indexes.

U.S. stock futures rose slightly but S&P 500 futures were largely flat, while Nasdaq 100 futures rose 0.2%. Those rises came after both indexes posted their best days since August on Monday, driven by falling oil prices.

title: Trump to address the U.N. General Assembly as Iran war rumbles on
summary: President Donald Trump will deliver a speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York City on Tuesday.
story: President Donald Trump will deliver a speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York City on Tuesday.

U.N. Ambassador Mike Waltz told reporters that the remarks would highlight peace deals the president has worked on, U.S. actions in the Western Hemisphere and progress on Trump’s 20-point peace plan in Gaza. It will also touch on the “importance of ensuring that Iran never has a nuclear weapon,” Waltz said.
The American president traditionally addresses the General Assembly each year.

In 2025, Trump spoke for almost an hour, criticizing climate change and European immigration policies. But what grabbed headlines were mishaps before and during his appearance at the U.N., as the escalator carrying Trump and first lady Melania Trump abruptly stopped and then the teleprompter with Trump’s speech broke early on in his remarks and he was forced to improvise.

Trump at the time blamed the world body, insinuating intentional sabotage to humiliate him, while U.N. officials said the White House’s videographer “may have inadvertently triggered the safety function” on the escalator.

Trump’s remarks to the assembly this year come as the U.N.’s Human Rights Council found in a report last week “reasonable grounds to believe” that the U.S. had committed war crimes during “indiscriminate attacks” against an Iranian school and a residential area in February.

Trump is expected to meet with several world leaders this week on the sidelines of the U.N. gathering, including Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez. It will be Rodríguez’s first meeting with Trump since the U.S. captured then-Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, who are in a Brooklyn jail awaiting trial.

Trump is also expected to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has said the meeting “could change a lot,” adding that there “is diplomatic momentum” in a push for an energy truce with the Kremlin.
Last week, Trump signed into law a Russian sanctions bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C.

He also announced that the U.S. would take over military operations and have “permanent control over security” in Greenland, in a deal expected to be signed Tuesday with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark to try and end the tense standoff over the strategic Arctic territory.

The U.N. assembly comes as the Iran war is about to enter its eighth month. Trump is expected to meet with leaders of the Gulf Cooperation Council, which includes Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday. Senior U.S. officials said Iran will be a key topic of conversation at the assembly this year.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the U.N. on Wednesday. Trump told Fox News that he would “probably” be open to meeting with Pezeshkian, but did not announce any specifics.

title: Iowa GOP Senate candidate calls for Iran war to end despite voting to let Trump continue it
summary: Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, has voted against House resolutions directing President Donald Trump to halt the war with Iran six times, including as recently as last week.
story: Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, has voted against House resolutions directing President Donald Trump to halt the war with Iran six times, including as recently as last week.
But on Monday, the Republican Senate candidate called for an “immediate end” to the conflict.

“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Hinson wrote on X, calling for measures like suspending the gas tax, pausing diesel exports and replenishing the highway trust fund to provide relief from high costs.
“These actions to lower costs are needed ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end,” she said.
It drew a quick response from her Democratic opponent, Josh Turek, who also pointed to a seventh vote by Hinson against ending U.S. hostilities in Lebanon as part of the conflict in the Middle East.
In a reply to Hinson, Turek wrote on X, “it’s easy to send a tweet but when you had the chance to vote to end this war, you chose not to.”

“You voted seven times to continue it, including just last week. It’s time to actually end the forever wars and put Iowa and Iowans first,” Turek continued. “Glad you’re finally following my lead after waffling on the proposals I put forward last week to address the rising costs of the war in Iran.”

Last month, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter shifted its Iowa Senate race rating from “lean Republican” to “toss-up.” Trump won the state in the last three presidential elections, and Democrats haven’t won a Senate race there since 2008.
Hinson’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment about her prior votes against the Iran war powers measures in the House.

The latest resolution passed the House 220-204 last Tuesday, with seven Republicans joining all Democrats present in supporting it. Among those seven were Reps. Zach Nunn and Marianette Miller-Meeks of Iowa, who had previously opposed such measures but changed their position.
Both are running for re-election in battleground House districts. The Cook Political Report rates their races as “toss-ups.”

Hinson, a three-term congresswoman, has been increasingly characterizing herself as “bipartisan” and slowly distancing herself from the Trump administration as polls show voters disapprove of the president’s handling of the war and the economy. Her messaging and votes highlight the difficult balance of turning out Trump’s strongest supporters while appealing to the growing number of voters who have soured on him.

Last month, Hinson objected to his proposal to import more foreign beef. Last week, when Vice President JD Vance went to Council Bluffs, Iowa, to rally for Republicans, Hinson did not attend, citing a scheduling conflict.

“I want to make a shoutout to an amazing public servant,” Vance said in his remarks. “I know she couldn’t be here today, but are we going to elect Ashley Hinson the next United States senator from the great state of Iowa?”
Meanwhile, another Midwest Republican Senate candidate running in a tough race on Tuesday said the Iran war must end.
Former Rep. Mike Rogers said in a video released on social media that “the war with Iran needs to end and end quickly.”
“When it does, energy costs will plummet,” Rogers said. “But Michigan families can’t afford to wait for that to happen.”
Similar to Hinson, Rogers said he supported suspending the state and federal gas tax and a temporary embargo on American diesel exports.
In response, Rogers’ Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed said on X, “You’ve spent your entire campaign supporting the war in Iran. Liar, coward, fraud.”

title: Tehran warns of ‘new weapons’ as Trump weighs meeting with Iranian president
summary: Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend.
story: Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend.

“If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Monday, according to the semiofficial Fars news agency.
Mohebbi did not provide details on what the new weapons were or which new locations could be hit.

Earlier, Trump said he would “probably” be open to meeting with his Iranian counterpart, President Masoud Pezeshkian, during the United Nations General Assembly this week, Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reported Sunday.

The possibility of a meeting offered a glimmer of hope for a resolution to the nearly seven-month war with Iran, which has resulted in Iran blocking the key Strait of Hormuz, and its Yemeni allies bombing a crucial east-west oil pipeline and threatening another crucial waterway. Resultant economic shock waves have hit the U.S. and the world economy, driving up oil and diesel prices and fueling inflation.

title: U.S. proposes AI alert system with China ahead of Trump-Xi summit
summary: The United States has proposed a new AI safety notification mechanism for President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to consider at their summit in Washington this week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday.
story: HONG KONG — The United States has proposed a new AI safety notification mechanism for President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to consider at their summit in Washington this week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday, amid global concern over whether the world’s two leading AI powers can work together to contain the technology’s potential dangers.

Speaking to reporters after daylong talks in New York with Chinese officials, Bessent said the two sides had discussed setting up a new U.S.-China AI dialogue that would include a mechanism for alerting each other to AI-related incidents that could affect national security.

“We think that just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important,” he said, adding that the two sides had agreed to meet again on the AI issue.
'Godfather of AI': Congress has about a year to get ahead of AI

AI is expected to be high on the agenda when Trump and Xi meet Thursday, especially after warnings from AI leaders in the U.S. that the technology could pose an existential threat within a few years. Trump has dismissed such concerns as a “hoax” while agreeing with AI executives such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that the U.S. must not allow China to pull ahead in the global AI race.

Experts caution that the Trump-Xi summit is unlikely to produce any major agreement on AI, citing the high level of distrust between the two countries. China has interpreted calls to slow down AI development as targeted at its own progress.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters that AI talks would not affect U.S. export controls on advanced chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment that have hindered Chinese AI companies.

Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng and China’s chief trade negotiator, Li Chenggang, did not comment to reporters as they left the talks at JPMorganChase headquarters. A Chinese readout of the talks published by Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency, did not mention the U.S. proposal and said only that the two sides had discussed AI.

Xinhua said the two sides also had “frank, in-depth and constructive exchanges on important economic and trade issues of common concern, including implementing the consensus reached in previous trade consultations and promoting bilateral trade and investment.”
A major question ahead of this week’s summit is whether Trump and Xi will agree to extend a fragile trade truce that is set to expire Nov. 10.

Bessent and Greer said the two sides had agreed to operationalize a new “Board of Trade” that was announced during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, and were exploring the potential for lower tariffs on “non-sensitive” products.

On the Chinese side, Greer said, those could include consumer goods and low-tech items, while U.S. exports of energy, agricultural goods and medical devices are also being considered. He did not say whether that meant tariffs on those items would be lowered now or that they would only be exempted from fresh duties in the future.

“There is a world where you have a relatively small subset of American and Chinese goods that can be traded in a balanced way that are non-sensitive,” he said. “Then in the future, as trade actions come up, we can consider them as a class unto themselves.”
Jennifer Jett reported from Hong Kong, and Steve Kopack and Allie Canal reported from New York.

title: Three dead in Moscow as Ukraine launches massive drone attack while Russia votes
summary: The largest Ukrainian drone attack reported so far on the Moscow region killed two people ⁠and damaged part of an oil refinery in the capital, authorities said Sunday.
story: Ukraine launched hundreds of drones at Moscow on Sunday, killing two people on the final day of a Russian parliamentary election that President Vladimir Putin has cast as a test of support for the war in ⁠Ukraine.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram: “In the Moscow region tonight, our long-range responses hit very noticeably. One of the key enterprises of Russia’s oil industry and an aggressor logistics facility were struck.”
He did not specifically mention the ongoing State Duma election, but added that Moscow could “end its brutal war and choose peace” if there is “political will” to do so.
An oil refinery was damaged in the strike, with videos showing smoke billowing out across the city.
In the village of Sofyino, ‌south of Moscow, a body covered in a stained ‌blanket lay in front of a damaged apartment block, the upper windows of which were blown out.
“Glass went flying, people started screaming and shouting. I turned around and the entrance doors had already been blown out, ⁠debris everywhere,” said resident Vitaliy, who gave only his first name.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said over 1,600 drones had been shot down by Russia since Saturday, including 450 heading toward Moscow.
In a Telegram post, he said: “This unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed.”

Moscow region governor Andrey Vorobyov said in a Telegram post that a 74-year-old man in the Orekhovo-Zuyevo District and a 44-year-old woman in Ramenskoye were killed in the attack. A third person later died of their injuries.
He said 15 people were hospitalized, including two teenagers, ages 14 and 15.
In a post on X, Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said: “My morning today started with congratulations from many foreign colleagues on Moscow Burning Day.”
He added: “Now that the war has come home, Russians have only Putin to blame for it. The message to him is simple: look out the Kremlin window, see the flames over Moscow — and end this war.”
At the same time, Russia continued its strikes on Ukraine, with three children and a woman killed in strikes in the Kyiv region, regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said in a Telegram post.

Kyiv has demonstrated an increasing ability to strike deep inside Russia in recent months, targeting key military and industrial sites as part of an effort to make everyday Russians feel the cost of the war. Russia has hammered Ukrainian cities across the conflict, now in its fifth year.
The State Duma vote, the first since Russia’s full-scale invasion, is expected to see Putin’s United Russia party easily retain ​its ⁠dominance in a process that critics deride as a farce.
The Kremlin is likely to present the outcome as evidence of public backing for Putin’s policies and for the war.

“Participation in the elections is our joint contribution to Russia’s victory,” Putin declared in a video address to the nation days before the vote. It will serve as a reminder that “millions of people are backing our fighters and that we stand together,” he added.

Election authorities say the ⁠three days of voting have proceeded smoothly despite reported cyberattacks on Saturday. Turnout by late morning on Sunday was at over 45% for the ​Duma vote and ⁠regional elections, said Central Election Commission Chairwoman Ella Pamfilova.
Most anti-war ‌candidates have been barred from the ballot.

Anti-war politician Boris Nadezhdin, who tried to challenge Putin in the presidential election two years ago but was barred from running, told NBC News earlier this week that the elections were “crooked” with no trace of real opposition, though he said disapproval could manifest in a higher number of spoiled ballots or increased tactical voting against Putin’s United Russia party.

Figures from the anti-war Yabloko party said they feared for their freedom after courts handed long jail terms to two senior party figures before the ‌vote. Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake ‌news is punishable by lengthy prison sentences.
In a small act of defiance, Yabloko’s leader, Nikolai Rybakov, demonstrably spoiled his ballot paper, writing his party’s name and the slogan “For peace.”

“No one in the world can claim anymore that everyone in Russia supports what is happening,” Rybakov told NBC News last week. “Now everyone has seen that millions of people disagree with what’s going on, and they have turned their attention to Yabloko precisely because it consistently advocates for peace and for an alternative to the status quo.”

Russian electoral officials said Saturday that an online voting system in Moscow had come under cyberattack. Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, has dismissed the Russian vote as a “pseudo election.”

Despite what experts see as the election’s predictable outcome, the NEST think tank in Berlin, co-founded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky, said the vote could ‌still produce awkward moments for the Kremlin at a time of economic strain.

“The consequences of the war are increasingly being felt within the ​country, and accumulated anxiety and frustration may translate into votes for the systemic opposition parties that the Kremlin has allowed to remain on ‌the ballot,” it said in a note.
Initial results are expected to start emerging at around 2 p.m. ET on Sunday, with more complete results available on Monday.

title: Princess Diana’s brother says King Charles ‘gaslit’ him in dispute over book claims
summary: Princess Diana’s brother, Charles Spencer, has accused King Charles of gaslighting him after Buckingham Palace pushed back at his claims about the monarch’s conduct.
story: Princess Diana’s brother, Charles Spencer, has accused King Charles of gaslighting him after Buckingham Palace pushed back at his claims about the monarch’s conduct.

Buckingham Palace released an unusually forceful statement Wednesday ahead of the release of a memoir by Spencer, which charts the breakdown of then-Prince Charles’ marriage to Princess Diana, and the fallout from her death in a Paris car crash in 1997, one year after the royal couple finalized their divorce.

In an initial excerpt released ahead of publication, Spencer recalled a heated phone call with Charles amid a disagreement about funeral arrangements, claiming that a furious Charles had told him Diana would “soon be forgotten.”

“While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” the palace had responded.
In an interview with Britain’s Mail on Sunday newspaper, Spencer said: “It is not every day you wake up to find you’ve been gaslit by the king.”
“It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I’d lied without the king being able to deny what I’d said,” Spencer added.
“Gaslighting” is a form of manipulation where the manipulator is trying to get someone to question their own reality, memory or perceptions.
In a further interview with the BBC that aired Sunday, Spencer said he told close friends and family at the time about what Charles had said “because it was so monstrous.”
He also appeared to indicate that Charles and Diana’s sons, heir to the throne Prince William and his brother, Prince Harry, were aware of his allegation before the memoir was published.
“I don’t like to talk about what I’ve been speaking about to William and Harry, but this will not be a surprise to them, I will tell you that. These words will not be a surprise to them,” he said.
There has been no public comment from William or Harry on Spencer’s memoir.

Spencer, an earl whose aristocratic family has generational ties with Britain’s royal family, denied that the book, published after years of silence, was motivated by money or score-settling. “I have a duty, as an eyewitness to history, in the final season of my life,” he told the BBC. “I wanted to just put things down that were true.”

He added: “This is not a threat, it’s a fact: I know lots of things about the king which I chose not to include in the book, because they were not relevant. I’m a historian. ... I wanted to give the context.”
Spencer’s book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” is due to be released publicly on Tuesday.

In other excerpts from the book, published in advance by the Daily Mail newspaper, Spencer writes that Charles sounded “giddily elated” and “like a lottery winner” when they spoke by phone immediately after Diana’s death, adding: “I suspect the prince’s first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not.”
He also speaks about his sister’s mental health and recounts conversations with her, saying she had told him how “things became very difficult indeed in the marriage early on.”

The book also includes an allegation that Diana suspected Charles was “in love with” a member of royal staff during their marriage, separate from his relationship with the now-Queen Camilla, though Spencer says he has no evidence that was true.
Since its initial statement, Buckingham Palace has remained silent on the further allegations in Spencer’s book. The palace again declined to comment Sunday.

Prince Harry, who quit as a working royal six years ago amid a reported rift with senior royals, has remained close to the Spencer family, with his own memoir “Spare” thanking “my mother’s siblings for their love, support, time, and perspective.”

Of his relationship with Harry, Spencer said: “There’s this perception in the media that I’m on Harry’s side. Well, I’m on my deceased sister’s sons’ side, both of them, and if either of them wanted anything, then I’d be equally there for them. I never get involved in one camp or the other, except as a benign figure, I hope.”
The royal family continued to undertake public duties this week even as Spencer’s book has dominated the headlines, with Charles also meeting with senior figures in AI at a summit in Scotland.

title: Diana’s brother says Charles sounded ‘giddily elated’ after her death
summary: Buckingham Palace remains gripped in drama as excerpts of Princess Diana’s brother’s book continues to be dripped into the public domain, ahead of its official release next week.
story: LONDON — King Charles III is facing more criticism from Princess Diana’s brother, Charles Spencer, with Buckingham Palace bracing for days of revelations from his tell-all memoir.

The latest advance excerpt from the book accuses the then-Prince Charles of sounding “giddily elated” and “like a lottery winner,” immediately after Diana’s death in a Paris car crash in 1997, one year after they finalized their divorce.

Spencer, an earl whose aristocratic family has generational ties with Britain’s royal family, writes that he was at his home in South Africa with his children when he learned “in the middle of the night” from his sister Jane Fellowes that Diana had been in a car crash. He later learned, “after escalating dread,” that she had died.

“The phone rang constantly. Prince Charles caught me as I crossed the landing upstairs,” he wrote. “Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he sounded giddily elated — like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time.”
On the call, Spencer wrote, Charles told him that he had informed Princes William and Harry, then 15 and 12, of their mother’s death.

“Looking back now, I suspect the prince’s first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not. It can be hard to feel too much sympathy for an ex-spouse, or those who care for them profoundly, after bitter divorce,” he added.

Spencer also detailed feeling shut out by royal protocol during Diana’s funeral arrangements, alleging that royal officials turned down a request to play music loved by Diana — Mozart’s “Requiem” —  during her funeral.
“Diana remained theirs, in Buckingham Palace’s eyes, even in death. Her family, despite her divorce, were simply expected to fall into line with any royal decisions,” he added.
In the first wave of revelations from the book earlier this week, Spencer alleged that Charles had told him that Diana would soon be forgotten in the days after her death.
Buckingham Palace released an unusually forceful statement denying Spencer’s claims and suggesting that grief for his older sister may have impacted his memory.

“While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” the statement said Wednesday.
A spokeswoman for Buckingham Palace declined to further comment Friday, telling NBC News that “we do not comment on books as a policy,” and referring to Wednesday’s statement.
Speaking to the BBC Friday, Spencer pushed back at the palace’s statement, maintaining: “I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said.”
Noting the wording of the palace statement, he added: “I don’t hear him saying he didn’t say that.”

Spencer’s book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” is due to be released publicly Tuesday. Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper is publishing excerpts in advance, while an interview with Spencer is due to air on CBS on Sunday.
Thursday’s tranche of new excerpts continued to provide difficult reading for the palace, reflecting on the breakdown of Diana and Charles’ marriage.
Spencer writes that his sister “told me that things became very difficult indeed in the marriage early on, and I am sure that both spouses despaired of the other at times.”
“I am not hypocritical enough to judge or criticise anyone else’s marital record. I am merely recording how my sister felt and am not assessing whether she was right or not,” he added.

Spencer also writes about Diana’s struggle with an eating disorder, which she spoke about during her lifetime, as well as her wider mental state, criticizing her transfer from a long-serving family doctor to a royal physician.

“It is a sad fact that, in her later years, Diana drove herself more than once to Beachy Head, the highest chalk sea cliff in England, while contemplating ending it all. Her love for her sons stopped her from going further,” he writes.
Add to Google
Add to Google

The royal family continued to undertake a busy schedule of public duties this week. Charles made headlines at an event meeting with senior figures in AI at a summit in Scotland, while the Prince and Princess of Wales, William and Kate, attended charitable events there.

Prince Harry, who returned to the United Kingdom last month but remains a nonworking member of the royal family, was also photographed for the first time since his return, at a charitable function Thursday.

Harry, whose own bombshell memoir “Spare” rattled the royal establishment in 2023, has remained close to the Spencer family, with his own book thanking “my mother’s siblings for their love, support, time, and perspective.”
He did not respond to questions shouted by reporters about his uncle’s book Thursday.

title: Trump administration grants visas to top Iranian leaders to attend U.N. General Assembly
summary: The decision to grant Iranian leaders visas to travel to New York City for the annual meeting of global leaders comes seven months into the U.S. war with Iran.
story: The Trump administration will allow an Iranian delegation to attend the United Nations General Assembly next week, albeit with some restrictions, a State Department spokesperson said Thursday.
The decision to grant Iranian top officials visas to travel to New York City for the annual meeting of global leaders comes seven months into the U.S. war with Iran.

“Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend U.N. General Assembly High Level Week,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy.”

The Iranian delegation’s trip comes at a sensitive time, as the U.S. military and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have continued attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the war.
President Donald Trump said Thursday that he is considering resuming full-scale attacks against Iran.
“I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not? It’s a big decision. Anything could happen with me,” Trump told Axios.
Last week, the U.S. military struck five Iranian tankers linked to the IRGC in response to attempted attacks on an American warship, according to U.S. Central Command.

The Iranian delegation cleared by the U.S. will be smaller than the one the country sent last year, the State Department said. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi will be a part of the delegation receiving U.S. visas, a U.S. source familiar with the decision said.

The U.S. has historically restricted the Iranian delegation’s travel during its visits to New York, but beginning in 2025 the Trump administration began blocking the officials’ access even to wholesale and luxury stores, confining their movements to “areas strictly necessary to transit to and from the U.N. headquarters district to conduct their official U.N. business,” according to the State Department.

“We will not let the Iranian regime’s elites exploit UNGA for a luxury retail splurge paid for by the Iranian people’s suffering, all while the regime funnels Iran’s wealth to support its terrorist proxies,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said Thursday on social media. “The U.S. will continue to ban Iranian UN Mission officials, visiting officials, and their dependents from buying wholesale club memberships or luxury goods here.”

Last month, an Iranian presidential protocol official said Tehran was still assessing the level and size of its attendance at the General Assembly this year, calling the conditions imposed by the U.S. illegal, without elaborating on the complaint.

The general debate of the General Assembly, the part of the meeting where world leaders will give speeches, will begin on Tuesday when Trump is expected to speak. Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the General Assembly on Wednesday.

Despite granting visas to the Iranian delegation, the Trump administration will once again block Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas from attending the General Assembly, according to a source familiar with the decision.

That decision is an extension of sanctions that deny the necessary visas to officials from the Palestinian Authority and the Palestine Liberation Organization to attend the annual meeting of global leaders, according to the source.

In a statement Wednesday, the State Department accused both organizations of trying to bypass negotiations by seeking unilateral recognition of a Palestinian state, taking actions to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict — including through the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice — and “glorifying acts of terrorism and terrorists in public pronouncements and school textbooks.”

The Palestinian Authority’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates rejected the U.S. decision and said in a statement that “the unjustified measure” runs counter to efforts aimed at restoring trust and “creating the political climate necessary to implement the two-state solution and achieve peace and stability in the region.”

title: King Charles issues fiery response to Princess Diana’s brother over claims in new book
summary: In a rare rebuke, Buckingham Palace issued a robust statement aimed at King Charles III’s former brother-in-law, Earl Charles Spencer, as he is set to release his bombshell memoir.
story: LONDON — Buckingham Palace has issued a rare and unusually forceful denial after the late Princess Diana’s brother claimed that the then-Prince Charles said his first wife would soon be forgotten in the days after her death.
In a soon-to-be-published memoir, Charles Spencer recounts the emotional days in the aftermath of Diana’s 1997 death in a Paris car crash at age 36.

An excerpt published Wednesday alleges a heated exchange with Charles, now the British king, over whether Princes William and Harry — then 15 and 12 — should walk behind their mother’s coffin in the funeral procession.

Spencer says he expressed that Diana would not want them to endure such an ordeal and claims that was met with a “stream of anger” from Charles. He writes that Charles “unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. ‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough.’”
Buckingham Palace replied with a forceful statement denying the claims and suggesting that grief for his older sister may have affected Spencer’s memory.

“While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” said the statement, released Wednesday.
Diana’s 1997 funeral procession is etched into modern memory.
Her brother and two young sons were among those who walked solemnly behind her coffin as it passed through central London.

India McTaggart, a royal correspondent at The Telegraph newspaper, told NBC News about Wednesday’s statement: “Earl Spencer’s book is expected to contain a number of incendiary claims, and perhaps this was the palace trying to get on the front foot and get ahead of some of the allegations we expect to see.”
The royal family mostly avoided commenting in 2023, when Prince Harry published his autobiography, “Spare,” which also generated global headlines with claims of bitter family feuds.

Queen Elizabeth II famously issued a brief but forceful statement in 2021 after Harry and his wife, Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, alleged racism in the family. “Recollections may vary,” the late queen said.
McTaggart said that “the palace will certainly be bracing for more headlines” as a result of the new memoir.
Add to Google
Add to Google

“At the same time, we’ll see Harry carrying out public engagements this week, while the king and the prince and princess of Wales continue with theirs. It will be interesting to see how all of that is covered now that they’re all in Britain at the same time.”

Diana was one of the most photographed women in the world after she married Charles in 1981. Their high-profile marriage ended in 1996, and she died a year later after being chased by paparazzi with her partner, Dodi Fayed. Her death in a Paris tunnel brought the world to a standstill.

At the time of her funeral, the royal family received criticism from the public and the media for appearing to be slow to react to the outpouring of love and grief from the public for a woman posthumously dubbed the “people’s princess.”
Spencer’s book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” is due to be published Tuesday. Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper is publishing excerpts in advance.
